# Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents

Muhang Tian    Sherry Yang Affiliation: New York University
Email: [mt4193@nyu.edu](mailto:)

###### Abstract

Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) techniques focus on maximizing
expected cumulative reward, where each action assumes to take a constant
unit of time. However, this assumption does not hold for agentic RL
tasks such as machine learning engineering (MLE) agents, where actions
involve data loading, feature engineering, and model training that take
variable durations. Efficiency matters in modern agentic RL where
actions are costly. To address this limitation, we adapt from
continuous-time RL and Semi-Markov Decision Process (SMDP) formulation
and propose Reward-rate Policy Gradient (RPG), where we focus on
optimizing the reward rate — the long-term reward per unit of time. RPG
estimates the reward rate from off-policy samples, then charges each
action for the time it consumes at that rate. We first conduct
theoretical analysis in the bandit setting to establish that RPG
approximates the optimal reward rate and empirically demonstrate it
outperforms baselines while avoiding enumeration over the policy space,
a known issue for an existing method. We then further apply RPG on a
small language model (Qwen3.5-4B) with self-improvement loops and
empirically show it obtains higher rewards within a fixed time budget
than vanilla RL on MLE-Bench and NanoGPT, with a 19.2% and 85.7% margin,
respectively. Our method provides a practical solution for optimizing
performance under wait time considerations in modern agentic RL tasks,
where actions interact with external environments and cost time.

## 1 Introduction

RL has been used extensively to train language models (LMs) and agents,
where the standard approach is to maximize expected cumulative reward
([Christiano et al., 2017](#bib.bib41); [Zhang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib3)). Recently, there has been interest in MLE agents,
where the goal is to automate the MLE pipeline to achieve best
performance on held-out data ([Chan et al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Yang et
al., 2025](#bib.bib15); [Nam et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)). Current
approaches mostly apply a strong LM in a search procedure: AIDE explores
the space of candidate programs as a tree ([Jiang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib34)), while MLE-STAR retrieves an initial solution with a
search engine and then refines its targeted components ([Nam et al.,
2026](#bib.bib1)). A separate line trains the model itself with RL on
performance score ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib15)). However, none of
these methods perform gradient updates that fundamentally change agents’
behavior to _learn_ to generate more efficient solutions. In MLE, each
action takes variable time and resources, so it is important to consider
samples’ costs for practicality — we want agents that are not only good,
but also _efficient_.

One solution is to use multi-objective RL and search for the Pareto
frontier between performance and time ([Roijers et al.,
2013](#bib.bib31); [Hayes et al., 2022](#bib.bib44)), but computing the
set of optimal solutions is often infeasible and compute-heavy ([Hayes
et al., 2022](#bib.bib44)). These limitations motivate an objective that
_intrinsically_ aims for long-run efficiency. One natural formulation is
the long-run reward per unit of time studied in Semi-Markov Decision
Process (SMDP) ([Sutton et al., 1999b](#bib.bib24); [Das et al.,
1999](#bib.bib12); [György et al., 2007](#bib.bib14)). Intuitively, the
method uses RL to maximize relative rewards, calculated from total
rewards minus the amount that it would have earned if time were spent
optimally. However, performing this computation requires knowing the
optimal reward rate apriori, which is often not the case in practice,
giving a chicken-or-egg dilemma. Existing approaches mainly use two ways
to tackle this. Directly optimizing the reward rate with SMDP policy
gradient objective ([Sutton et al., 1999a](#bib.bib9)) requires
estimating the rate of the current policy from on-policy rollouts, an
operation that is still expensive when actions are costly. The
continuous-time bandit approach ([György et al., 2007](#bib.bib14))
estimates the optimal reward rate from historical samples, but it
requires an exhaustive search over the policy space, infeasible in
modern agentic RL settings where action space is large.

To that end, we propose Reward-rate Policy Gradient (RPG), which uses
off-policy historical samples to estimate the reward rate under the
greedy policy and maximizes for relative reward
([Figure 1](#S1.F1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")).
RPG avoids the limitations of the two previous methods. It does not need
time-costly on-policy rollouts for each gradient step, and does not
require searching over the policy space. Additionally, RPG is simple to
adopt in the current RL pipeline, since it only requires a reward-rate
estimator and uses the relative reward as the learning signal. We first
study RPG in the bandit setting and theoretically prove that, in
expectation, if the greedy policy’s reward rate is estimated well, then
RPG is equivalent to the Dinkelbach iteration ([Dinkelbach,
1967](#bib.bib7); [Schaible, 1976](#bib.bib6)), and natural policy
gradient (NPG) ([Amari, 1998](#bib.bib30)) is suited for reward-rate
optimization due to preconditioning on Fisher information. Experiments
on the bandit setting confirm that RPG obtains lower regret than the
reward-rate upper-confidence-bound algorithm by [György et al.
(2007)](#bib.bib14) without the need to search over the policy space.
These findings motivate us to apply Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO),
a first-order approximation of NPG methods ([Kakade, 2001](#bib.bib29);
[Schulman et al., 2015](#bib.bib8)), on MLE-Bench and NanoGPT. Compared
against vanilla RL baselines on the same time budget, RPG shows a 19.2%
average improvement in performance across 20 out of 22 MLE-Bench tasks
and an 85.7% margin on NanoGPT. Our findings demonstrate that RPG is a
practical solution for future agentic RL frameworks where actions are
costly.

Figure 1: Overview of RPG in MLE, where our goal is to optimize for
reward per unit of time in agentic RL contexts. Our agent under policy
$`\pi_{\theta}`$ is asked to self-improve upon its previous MLE scripts
from buffer $`{\mathcal{B}}`$, and each action $`a`$ is a proposed
script that executes in variable time $`\delta`$ and admits a
performance score $`r`$ such as AUC. $`\hat{\rho}`$ is estimated from
past samples in buffer $`{\mathcal{B}}`$ and captures the cost per unit
of time. Relative reward $`\tilde{r}`$ is then used in PPO to perform RL
training. Maximizing the relative reward optimizes for reward rate,
giving higher reward per unit of time and more efficient RL agents.

## 2 Preliminaries

### 2.1 Semi-MDP Policy Gradient

We introduce the notation and setup for the SMDP setting where each
action takes a variable amount of time ([Sutton et al.,
1999b](#bib.bib24); [Das et al., 1999](#bib.bib12)). Let states be
$`s\in{\mathcal{S}}`$ and actions be $`a\in{\mathcal{A}}`$. At each step
$`t`$, the policy $`\pi(a_{t}\mid s_{t})`$ is a conditional distribution
on the actions. Taking the action $`a_{t}`$ gives reward
$`r_{t+1}:=r(s_{t},a_{t})`$ and time
$`\delta_{t+1}:=\delta(s_{t},a_{t})`$, and the transition model is a
joint conditional distribution
$`p(s_{t+1},\delta_{t+1},r_{t+1}\mid s_{t},a_{t})`$. Our objective is to
maximize the long-term reward per unit of time:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\rho(\pi)=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\big[\sum_{j=1}^{t}r_{j}\big]}{\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\big[\sum_{j=1}^{t}\delta_{j}\big]},\quad\pi^{*}=\argmax_{\pi}\rho(\pi).
``` |  | (1) |

For a parameterized policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$, taking the gradient gives

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\nabla_{\theta}\,\rho(\pi_{\theta})=\frac{\sum_{s}d^{\pi_{\theta}}(s)\sum_{a}\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)Q^{\pi_{\theta}}(s,a)}{\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}[\delta]},
``` |  | (2) |

where
$`Q^{\pi_{\theta}}(s,a)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}\big[r-\rho(\pi_{\theta})\,\delta+V^{\pi_{\theta}}(s^{\prime})\mid s,a\big]`$
is the differential action-value function (see full derivation in
[Section A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Semi-MDP Policy Gradient Theorem ‣ Appendix A Derivation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")).
Empirically, the division by $`\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}[\delta]`$ can
be dropped since modern adaptive optimizers like Adam ([Kingma and Ba,
2015](#bib.bib42)) and gradient clipping reduce its impact on the
gradients. Thus, the implementation is a straight-forward plug-in using
the relative reward $`\tilde{r}_{t}`$ into existing RL algorithms

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\tilde{r}_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle:=r_{t}-\hat{\rho}_{t}\,\delta_{t},\qquad e_{t}=\tilde{r}_{t}+V_{\phi}(s_{t+1})-V_{\phi}(s_{t}),\qquad\hat{A}_{t}=\sum_{l\geq 0}\lambda^{l}\,e_{t+l},`$ |  | (3) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\theta)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{t}\Big[\min\big\{w_{t}(\theta)\hat{A}_{t},\;\mathrm{clip}\big(w_{t}(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon\big)\hat{A}_{t}\big\}\Big],\qquad w_{t}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})},`$ |  | (4) |

where $`\hat{\rho}_{t}`$ is a Monte Carlo approximation of $`\rho(\pi)`$
from on-policy rollouts. Intuitively, the relative reward
$`\tilde{r}_{t}`$ is the gain obtained for the selected action when
$`\delta_{t}`$ units of time are used at a cost of $`\rho(\pi)`$, so
actions are ranked by their relative performance per unit of time.

### 2.2 Continuous Time Bandit

Reward-rate RL has also been studied in the continuous-time bandit
setting ([György et al., 2007](#bib.bib14)). The agent observes context
$`x_{t}`$ drawn i.i.d. from a fixed distribution on a finite set
$`{\mathcal{X}}`$, and each action $`a_{t}\in{\mathcal{A}}`$ yields a
reward $`r_{t+1}`$ and time $`\delta_{t+1}`$, with
$`r\in[r_{\min},r_{\max}]`$ and
$`\delta\in[\delta_{\min},\delta_{\max}]`$, $`\delta_{\min}>0`$. The
policy $`u\in{\mathcal{U}}=\{u:{\mathcal{X}}\to{\mathcal{A}}\}`$ is
assumed to be stationary and deterministic. Rewards
$`\{r_{j}\}_{j=1}^{t}`$ and durations $`\{\delta_{j}\}_{j=1}^{t}`$ are
drawn i.i.d. across steps from a fixed distribution given $`(x,a)`$. The
objective is to maximize the relative value under the optimal reward
rate:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q^{*}(x,a)\;=\;\mathbb{E}\big[r(x,a)\big]-\rho^{*}\,\mathbb{E}\big[\delta(x,a)\big],\qquad\rho^{*}=\max_{u\in{\mathcal{U}}}\rho(u),
``` |  | (5) |

so that a policy is optimal when it selects
$`a^{*}=\argmax_{a\in{\mathcal{A}}}q^{*}(x,a)`$ at every context. When
the reward rate is not optimal, $`\rho\neq\rho^{*}`$, we denote the
relative value as $`q_{\rho}(x,a)`$. Regret is thus defined as

|     |                                                             |     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       R_{t}=\rho^{*}\sum_{j=1}^{t}\delta_{j}-\sum_{j=1}^{t}r_{j}.
       ```                                                          |     | (6) |

To minimize regret, the algorithm starts by estimating $`\rho^{*}`$ with
$`\hat{\rho}_{t}`$ using the past history
$`\{(r_{j},\delta_{j})\}_{j=1}^{t}`$ and performs an exhaustive search
over all possible policies

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{\rho}_{t}=\max_{u\in{\mathcal{U}}}\,\big\{\bar{\rho}_{t}(u)-b_{t}(u)\big\},\qquad\bar{\rho}_{t}(u)=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{t}\mathbbm{1}\{a_{j-1}=u(x_{j-1})\}\,r_{j}}{\sum_{j=1}^{t}\mathbbm{1}\{a_{j-1}=u(x_{j-1})\}\,\delta_{j}},
``` |  | (7) |

which subtracts a confidence width $`b_{t}(u)`$, giving a lower bound
satisfying $`\hat{\rho}_{t}\leq\rho^{*}`$ with high probability. Actions
are then selected optimistically with the estimated relative value,
where $`\bar{r}_{t}`$ and $`\bar{\delta}_{t}`$ are sample averages and
$`c_{t}`$ is a confidence bonus

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
a_{t}=\argmax_{a\in{\mathcal{A}}}\;\big\{\bar{r}_{t}(x_{t},a)-\hat{\rho}_{t}\,\bar{\delta}_{t}(x_{t},a)+c_{t}(x_{t},a)\big\}.
``` |  | (8) |

This algorithm yields $`O(\log T)`$ expected regret bound but requires
enumerating $`|{\mathcal{U}}|=|{\mathcal{A}}|^{|{\mathcal{X}}|}`$
policies at each step. More details on the algorithm’s construction of
$`c_{t}`$ and $`b_{t}(u)`$ are in
[Section A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 More on ( ) ‣ Appendix A Derivation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").

## 3 Reward-rate Policy Gradient

In this section, we propose RPG for optimizing the reward rate
practically. We provide an outline for RPG in
[Section 3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Main Algorithm ‣ 3 Reward-rate Policy Gradient ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
that shows how we avoid previous algorithms’ limitations.
[Section 3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Theoretical Analysis ‣ 3 Reward-rate Policy Gradient ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
shares our theoretical insights, which were validated through
experiments in
[Section 3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Bandit Validation ‣ 3 Reward-rate Policy Gradient ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").

### 3.1 Main Algorithm

##### Current limitations.

We first describe limitations of current approaches and then share the
intuition behind our algorithm design. The SMDP policy gradient theorem
in
[Equation 2](#S2.E2 "In 2.1 Semi-MDP Policy Gradient ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
tells us it is viable to do gradient-based optimization on a
parameterized policy to maximize reward rate. However, the core
constraint in practice is that it requires multiple rollouts of the
on-policy trajectory $`\{(r_{j},\delta_{j})\}_{j=1}^{T}`$ to estimate
$`\rho(\pi)`$. Since the time $`\delta_{j}`$ for each step is variable
and costly, this makes the estimation take a long time, at least
$`\sum_{j\leq T}\delta_{j}`$, for each gradient update, making it
impractical for training efficient MLE agents. On the other hand, the
continuous-time bandit approach is an alternative by optimizing for the
relative reward using an off-policy reward rate estimate
$`\hat{\rho}_{t}`$
([Equation 7](#S2.E7 "In 2.2 Continuous Time Bandit ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")),
but the limitation being that it involves enumeration over all possible
policies.

##### Proposed algorithm.

Given the limitations discussed above, our design principle for creating
a practical reward-rate RL algorithm is as follows. We first use a
predictor $`f_{\rho}`$ fitted on the historical buffer $`{\mathcal{B}}`$
to approximate the reward rate and use the predicted rate $`\hat{\rho}`$
to calculate relative reward $`\tilde{r}`$. This design allows us to
avoid sampling on-policy long-horizon rollouts. Unlike the
continuous-time bandit setting where policies are deterministic ([György
et al., 2007](#bib.bib14)), LMs have stochastic policies, so we apply
policy gradient updates on expected relative reward to train LMs agents.
Our algorithm is shown in
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Proposed algorithm. ‣ 3.1 Main Algorithm ‣ 3 Reward-rate Policy Gradient ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").
Ideally, the reward-rate predictor $`f_{\rho}`$ should approximate the
optimal $`\rho^{*}`$, which then serves as $`\hat{\rho}`$ for the
relative reward. However, directly estimating
$`\hat{\rho}\approx\rho^{*}`$ is difficult, even in the bandit setting,
since it requires enumeration over the policy space. Thus, to make the
approach practical, we set $`f_{\rho}`$ to estimate the greedy policy’s
reward rate. This choice is supported by our results in the bandit
setting
([Sections 3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Theoretical Analysis ‣ 3 Reward-rate Policy Gradient ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
and [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Bandit Validation ‣ 3 Reward-rate Policy Gradient ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")),
where we demonstrate that a softmax policy with NPG updates converges to
the optimal $`\rho^{*}`$ through both theory and experiments.
Empirically on MLE-Bench and NanoGPT, we show that PPO also performs
well despite it being a first-order approximation of NPG. The estimator
$`f_{\rho}`$ can be anything that estimates the greedy reward rate, such
as Bayesian inference, Robbins-Monro iteration, or neural networks.

1: Policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$, greedy reward rate estimator $`f_{\rho}`$,
buffer $`{\mathcal{B}}`$, $`\hat{\rho}_{1}\leftarrow 0`$.

2: $`\triangleright`$  $`f_{\rho}`$ is a Normal-Inverse-Wishart (NIW)
posterior, but it can also be Robbins-Monro or neural
networks.  $`\triangleleft`$

### 3.2 Theoretical Analysis

##### Setup.

We share our findings in the bandit setting, which provides motivation
for approximating the greedy reward rate for $`\hat{\rho}`$ and using
PPO in our algorithm design. Our analysis is focused on the expected
setting with a softmax policy
$`\pi_{\theta}(a\mid x)=\exp(\theta_{a,x})/\sum_{b}\exp(\theta_{b,x})`$.
Our assumptions are as follows: (1) boundedness in reward and time, (2)
positive gap condition for relative value
$`\min_{x}\big[q^{*}(x,a^{*}(x))-\max_{a\neq a^{*}(x)}q^{*}(x,a)\big]>0`$,
and (3) contexts are drawn i.i.d. from $`p(x)`$. Details of the analysis
are in
[Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").

##### Approximate Dinkelbach iteration.

We first analyze under which conditions an arbitrary sequence of reward
rates $`\{\rho_{k}\}_{k=1}^{\infty}`$ would be near the optimal
$`\rho^{*}`$.
[Theorem 1](#Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 1. ‣ Approximate Dinkelbach iteration. ‣ 3.2 Theoretical Analysis ‣ 3 Reward-rate Policy Gradient ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
shows that if $`\rho_{k+1}`$ is within a asymmetric $`\gamma`$-tolerance
band around the greedy reward rate $`\rho(u_{\rho_{k}})`$ at every step
$`k\geq 2`$, then the sequence would be contained within an interval
around the optimal reward rate
$`\rho_{k}\in[(1-R\gamma/(1+\gamma))\rho^{*},(1+\gamma)\rho^{*}]`$ as
$`k\to\infty`$, which suggests we are approximately doing a Dinkelbach
iteration ([Dinkelbach, 1967](#bib.bib7)). When the estimation is exact,
$`\gamma=0`$, the sequence reaches $`\rho^{*}`$ in finite steps.
[Theorem 1](#Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 1. ‣ Approximate Dinkelbach iteration. ‣ 3.2 Theoretical Analysis ‣ 3 Reward-rate Policy Gradient ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
suggests that we can use an estimation of the greedy reward rate as
$`\hat{\rho}`$ for relative reward calculation and iterate greedily to
approximate $`\rho^{*}`$. This finding holds tremendous value in
practice, since predicting the greedy reward rate at the current
$`\rho_{k}`$ is an easier task than estimating $`\rho^{*}`$, where the
latter requires exhaustive search over the policy space but the former
can be approximated with historical samples in $`{\mathcal{B}}`$ by
selecting top solutions according to
$`\tilde{r}(\rho_{k})=r-\rho_{k}\,\delta`$.

###### Theorem 1.

Let $`\gamma\in[0,1]`$ be a tolerance term,
$`\rho_{1}\in[0,\rho_{\max}]`$, and
$`\chi:=1-\delta_{\min}/\delta_{\max}\in(0,1)`$. For every $`k\geq 1`$,
let $`u_{\rho_{k}}(x)\in\argmax_{a}q_{\rho_{k}}(x,a)`$ be a greedy
policy under any tie-breaking and $`\rho(u_{\rho_{k}})`$ is the reward
rate of the greedy policy, let $`\tilde{\rho}_{k+1}`$ be any value with
the sequence satisfying the condition
$`\rho(u_{\rho_{k}})/(1+\gamma)\leq\tilde{\rho}_{k+1}\leq(1+\gamma)\,\rho(u_{\rho_{k}})`$,
$`\rho_{k+1}=\mathrm{clip}_{[0,\rho_{\max}]}(\tilde{\rho}_{k+1})`$ where
$`\mathrm{clip}_{[0,\rho_{\max}]}(z):=\min\{\max\{z,0\},\,\rho_{\max}\}`$,
$`\rho_{\max}=r_{\max}/\delta_{\min}`$. Then, for every $`k\geq 2`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho_{k}\in\Big[\big(1-R\gamma/(1+\gamma)\big)\rho^{*}-\big(\chi/(1+\gamma)\big)^{k-2}\rho_{\max},\,(1+\gamma)\rho^{*}\Big],
``` |  | (9) |

where $`R=\delta_{\max}/\delta_{\min}>1`$. If $`\gamma=0`$, then the
sequence increases monotonically
$`\rho_{2}\leq\rho_{3}\leq\cdots\leq\rho^{*}`$ and the iteration reaches
$`\rho_{k}=\rho^{*}`$ after finite steps.

##### NPG and reward-rate RL.

[Theorem 1](#Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 1. ‣ Approximate Dinkelbach iteration. ‣ 3.2 Theoretical Analysis ‣ 3 Reward-rate Policy Gradient ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
suggests that if the predicted rate approximates the greedy rate, then
it would be contained within an interval around the optimal
$`\rho^{*}`$, but it does not make any statements about the training
dynamics, so we further analyze the behavior of $`\pi_{\theta}`$. Define
$`A_{\theta}(\rho,x)=(q_{\rho}(x,\cdot)-\langle\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x),q_{\rho}(x,\cdot)\rangle\,{\bm{1}})`$,
where $`{\bm{1}}=[1\ldots 1]\in\mathbb{R}^{|{\mathcal{A}}|}`$. The
gradient update rules are

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\theta^{\prime}_{x}\leftarrow\theta_{x}+\eta\,A_{\theta}(\rho,x)\quad\text{(NPG)},\quad\theta^{\prime}_{x}\leftarrow\theta_{x}+\eta\,\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\odot A_{\theta}(\rho,x)\quad\text{(Standard PG)}.
``` |  |

We thus hypothesize that NPG is more suited for reward-rate RL since it
has less coupling between $`\pi_{\theta}`$ and the magnitude of
$`A_{\theta}`$. Coupling would be undesirable since $`\theta_{x}`$ is
updated proportionally to the policy weight
$`\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)`$, reducing the signal for actions with
large advantage $`A_{\theta}`$ but low $`\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)`$¹¹ 1
In standard RL setting, this finding has already been observed [Kakade
(2001)](#bib.bib29), but in reward-rate RL, $`A_{\theta}`$ is a function
of $`\rho`$ which is estimated from policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$, so the
amount of coupling is stronger.. We establish the validity of NPG
updates in
[Theorem 2](#Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 2. ‣ NPG and reward-rate RL. ‣ 3.2 Theoretical Analysis ‣ 3 Reward-rate Policy Gradient ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").
It shows that the natural gradient updates are equivalent to a Boltzmann
policy on the relative value $`q_{\bar{\rho}_{k}}(x,a)`$ with a running
average rate $`\bar{\rho}_{k}`$. If $`\rho_{1}`$ is initialized within
$`[0,\rho^{*}]`$, and greedy reward rate estimation is exact
$`\rho_{k+1}=\rho(u_{\bar{\rho}_{k}})`$, then the error between
$`\bar{\rho}_{k}`$ and $`\rho^{*}`$ shrinks in $`O(k^{-(1-\chi)})`$.
Furthermore, when $`\bar{\rho}_{k}`$ is within $`\bar{\varepsilon}`$ of
$`\rho^{*}`$, which
[Equation 10](#S3.E10 "In Theorem 2. ‣ NPG and reward-rate RL. ‣ 3.2 Theoretical Analysis ‣ 3 Reward-rate Policy Gradient ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
guarantees after finitely many steps, the greedy action at
$`\bar{\rho}_{k}`$ becomes the optimal one, and the policy increases the
optimal arm’s probability towards $`1`$. This finding suggests that NPG
methods bring performance benefits in reward-rate RL and motivates us to
apply PPO in practice, a first-order approximation of NPG ([Schulman et
al., 2017](#bib.bib10)).

###### Theorem 2.

Let $`\rho_{1},\rho_{2},\ldots`$ be a sequence of reward rates and let
$`\theta^{(k)}`$ be the softmax logits after $`k`$ NPG update steps with
learning rate $`\eta`$ from the zero initialization, with
$`\bar{\rho}_{k}=\sum_{n\leq k}\rho_{n}/k`$. Then for every $`x`$ and
$`k\geq 1`$, $`\pi_{\theta^{(k)}}`$ is the Boltzmann policy of
$`q_{\bar{\rho}_{k}}(x,a)`$ with inverse temperature $`\eta k`$. If
moreover $`\rho_{1}\in[0,\rho^{*}]`$ and
$`\rho_{k+1}=\rho(u_{\bar{\rho}_{k}})`$, then $`\bar{\rho}_{k}`$
increases to $`\rho^{*}`$ in $`O(k^{-(1-\chi)})`$

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho^{*}-\bar{\rho}_{k}\;\leq\;(\rho^{*}-\bar{\rho}_{1})\,\exp(1-\chi)\,(k+1)^{-(1-\chi)}.
``` |  | (10) |

Furthermore, let
$`\delta_{\mathrm{spr}}\in(0,\delta_{\max}-\delta_{\min}]`$ be the
maximum time gap, and $`\Delta^{*}`$ be the minimum relative value gap
under $`\rho^{*}`$, define
$`\bar{\varepsilon}:=\Delta^{*}/(2\delta_{\mathrm{spr}})`$, for every
$`k\geq k_{0}`$, the greedy policy is optimal

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\pi_{\theta^{(k)}}(a^{*}\mid x)\geq 1-(|{\mathcal{A}}|-1)\,\exp\big({-\eta\,\Delta^{*}k/2}\big),\quad k_{0}:=\Big\lceil\big(\exp(1-\chi)\,(\rho^{*}-\bar{\rho}_{1})/\bar{\varepsilon}\big)^{1/(1-\chi)}\Big\rceil.
``` |  | (11) |

### 3.3 Bandit Validation

![Refer to caption](2609.36393v1/figures/bandit/legend_strip_all.png)

(a) 4 contexts $`|{\mathcal{X}}|=4`$.

(b) 64 contexts $`|{\mathcal{X}}|=64`$.

Figure 2: Our proposed approach NPG-NIW obtains similar or lower regret
than C-UCB while avoiding exhaustive search over policies. Standard
policy gradient (SPG-NIW) also performs worse than NPG, verifying our
theory that NPG’s decoupling helps reward-rate RL. y-axis is regret at
the final step over $`100`$ trials, x-axis is the number of arms $`K`$,
and 4 environments are considered: (E1) independent reward and time,
(E2) time and reward have $`0.8`$ correlation, (E3) time and reward have
$`-0.8`$ correlation, and (E4) reward and time are lognormal with
$`+0.5`$ correlation.

Our theory suggests that NPG has a decoupling effect on reward-rate
optimization, and using greedy reward rate as $`\hat{\rho}`$ can also
approximate the optimal rate as iterations grow. The former brings
performance benefits, whereas the latter is a feasibility benefit in
large action and context spaces where an exhaustive search over the
policy space is intractable. We conduct experiments to examine whether
these benefits hold true in practice. Our finding is in
[Figure 2](#S3.F2 "In 3.3 Bandit Validation ‣ 3 Reward-rate Policy Gradient ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents"),
and NPG-NIW uses softmax policy with NPG updates and NIW posterior
fitted on greedy historical samples for $`\hat{\rho}`$ estimation.
Continuous-time upper confidence bound (C-UCB) is the approach by
[György et al. (2007)](#bib.bib14). We first observe that if we use
C-UCB’s constants exactly as in the paper, it breaks since the constants
are too large (C-UCB, theory), but treating them as tunable
hyperparameters allows it to work (C-UCB, tuned). When only having small
context and action spaces
([Figure 2(a)](#S3.F2.sf1 "In Figure 2 ‣ 3.3 Bandit Validation ‣ 3 Reward-rate Policy Gradient ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")),
C-UCB uses exhaustive search for $`\hat{\rho}`$ estimation. When the
context and action space is large
([Figure 2(b)](#S3.F2.sf2 "In Figure 2 ‣ 3.3 Bandit Validation ‣ 3 Reward-rate Policy Gradient ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")),
C-UCB cannot afford to enumerate over all policies, so we use an
approximation where 2048 policies are drawn uniformly at random from
past visited ones to predict $`\hat{\rho}`$. Across both settings, we
observe that NPG-NIW obtains lower or similar regret as C-UCB baselines,
thus confirming our hypothesis that greedy reward rate estimation can be
used for $`\hat{\rho}`$ without enumerating the policy space. When
comparing NPG with standard policy gradient updates (SPG-NIW), we
observe that it consistently obtains higher regret than NPG, supporting
our theoretical finding that NPG provides performance benefits. More
experiments and implementation details are in
[Sections C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Bandit Experiments ‣ Appendix C Implementation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents"),
[D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 Bandit Experiments, |𝒳|=4 ‣ Appendix D Experiments ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
and [D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Bandit Experiments, |𝒳|>4 ‣ Appendix D Experiments ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").

## 4 Reward-rate for MLE Agent

In this section, we present our results demonstrating that RPG finds
good solutions in less time than vanilla RL, suggesting that reward-rate
RL is a practical solution for training efficient agents. We provide our
empirical results on MLE-Bench and NanoGPT in
[Sections 4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Evaluation Results on MLE-Bench ‣ 4 Reward-rate for MLE Agent ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
and [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Evaluation Results on NanoGPT ‣ 4 Reward-rate for MLE Agent ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").

### 4.1 Instantiating Language Models for Reward-rate Policies

##### Environment setup.

The theory in
[Section 3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Theoretical Analysis ‣ 3 Reward-rate Policy Gradient ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
suggests that we should approximate the greedy reward rate for
$`\hat{\rho}`$ and use PPO for training, but training MLE agents also
requires deliberate environment setup, which we share in this section.
We start with a base prompt as our initial state $`s_{0}`$ containing
task descriptions such as data loading path, meaning of features, and
the performance metric used for the evaluation. We also explicitly ask
the LM agent to take efficiency into consideration by encouraging it to
use a subset of features. An action $`a_{0}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s_{0})`$ is
the generated script by the agent, and the code is executed in a sandbox
environment to produce time $`\delta_{1}`$ and reward $`r_{1}`$. If the
script successfully executes, $`r_{1}`$ would be a performance score. A
timeout budget $`\delta_{\max}`$ is set as the upper limit of the time
allowed for script execution. For scripts that fail to run, such as when
they have a bug, we encounter trouble assigning their reward rate since
their reward is $`0`$ and $`\tilde{r}=-\hat{\rho}\,\delta`$ is maximized
by $`\delta\to 0`$. This implies a script that fails on its first line
dominates all honest attempts. Thus, we charge every failure the full
time limit $`\delta_{\max}`$ and a constant penalty of $`-10`$,
preventing the policy from reward-hacking by failing fast, and
executable scripts have higher rewards than non-executable ones.

##### State transition with self-improvement.

Besides setting up the environment and reward properly, we also want our
agent to improve based on its own previous attempts, so we would ideally
have a self-improving agent making progress on the task over time. We
discuss how we connect the agent’s own solutions to form
self-improvement loops. At every step, we store the observed transition
$`(a_{t},r_{t+1},\delta_{t+1})`$ into the buffer $`{\mathcal{B}}`$. The
next state $`s_{t+1}`$ is constructed by concatenating the base prompt
$`s_{0}`$ with the previous code $`a^{\prime}`$ and a self-improvement
phrase $`i_{0}`$ explicitly asking the agent to improve upon the
performance score $`r^{\prime}`$ and time $`\delta^{\prime}`$. The
selection of $`(a^{\prime},r^{\prime},\delta^{\prime})`$ from buffer
$`{\mathcal{B}}`$ is based on a top-$`k`$ selection according to the
relative reward
$`\tilde{r}(\hat{\rho}_{t+1})=r^{\prime}-\hat{\rho}_{t+1}\,\delta^{\prime}`$.
This naturally gives a self-improvement chain where the agent is tasked
with making progress on its best proposed solutions observed thus far.

##### Reward-rate predictor.

At each step $`t`$, our agent uses its history of attempts to predict
the reward rate $`\hat{\rho}`$. The reward-rate estimator $`f_{\rho}`$
is a NIW posterior with joint Gaussian likelihood ([Murphy,
2012](#bib.bib38)) fitted from historical samples observed in buffer
$`{\mathcal{B}}`$. We model the pair as
$`(r_{\mathrm{acc}},\log\delta_{\mathrm{acc}})`$, where
$`r_{\mathrm{acc}}`$ and $`\delta_{\mathrm{acc}}`$ are the accumulated
reward and time, and we take the logarithm because we need time to be
positive. We fit the posterior at each step, and sample $`M`$ reward
rates from it and take the 95th percentile
$`\hat{\rho}_{t+1}=\mathrm{Quantile}_{0.95}(\{\rho_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M})`$.
More details are in
[Section C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Reward-rate Predictor ‣ Appendix C Implementation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").

### 4.2 Evaluation Results on MLE-Bench

We provide our results for MLE-Bench in
[Table 1](#S4.T1 "In Reward-rate predictor. ‣ 4.1 Instantiating Language Models for Reward-rate Policies ‣ 4 Reward-rate for MLE Agent ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").
We use Qwen3.5-4B as our LM and apply the method in
[Section 4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Instantiating Language Models for Reward-rate Policies ‣ 4 Reward-rate for MLE Agent ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").
Our baseline is vanilla RL, where rewards are performance scores only
and time budget is $`\delta_{\max}`$. We run RPG and the baseline until
convergence. Our evaluation metric is the mean reward obtained by the
self-improvement chains at every time budget. Specifically, at every
step, there are batch_size self-improvement chains, and for each chain,
a time $`\delta`$ and reward $`r`$ are earned. We calculate the mean
reward $`r`$ across chains at every cumulative time budget
$`t\in[0,200,\ldots,T]`$ with $`200`$-second intervals. The final time
$`T`$ is decided by taking the cumulative time containing 95% of the
self-improvement chains. Each task is evaluated with three repetitions.
Across the $`22`$ tasks RPG show an average 19.2% improvement over
vanilla at the final time budget, after dropping the task with highest
and lowest improvements. The two methods’ proposed MLE scripts have
distinct differences in wall clock time. An example of the budget curve
along with the generated script is shown in
[Figure 3](#S4.F3 "In Reward-rate predictor. ‣ 4.1 Instantiating Language Models for Reward-rate Policies ‣ 4 Reward-rate for MLE Agent ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
for the spooky-author task. Vanilla uses a concatenation of different
features and trains a gradient-boosted tree in 13 seconds with log loss
0.727, whereas RPG uses count features along with logistic regression to
obtain 0.469 log loss in 5 seconds. The budget curve behind every task
is provided in
[Section D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 MLE Agent ‣ Appendix D Experiments ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents"),
and implementation details are in
[Section C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 MLE-Bench ‣ Appendix C Implementation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").

### 4.3 Evaluation Results on NanoGPT

Figure 4: Budget curve and an example self-improvement step on NanoGPT.
(Left) At the final budget, RPG improves over vanilla by $`85.7\%`$.
(Right) Example of a self-improvement edit by RPG, which rewrites
Newton–Schulz in the Muon optimizer as a triton kernel with a compiled
iteration and adds a learning-rate warmup. The new edit crosses the loss
target in less time.

##### Motivation and setup.

The MLE-Bench setting discussed above is based on Kaggle competitions.
To extend the scope of reward-rate RL agents, we also apply RPG to the
NanoGPT speedrun challenge ([Karpathy, 2022](#bib.bib32); [Jordan et
al., 2024](#bib.bib33)), where the task is to train a tiny LM down to a
validation cross-entropy loss of $`3.28`$ on FineWeb ([Penedo et al.,
2024](#bib.bib37)) with eight GPUs as fast as possible. This task makes
the time taken to reach the $`3.28`$ target loss a natural choice to
optimize for. Thus, as a baseline, we implement vanilla RL using time to
reach the $`3.28`$ target loss as reward, and compare with RPG using
relative reward as the learning signal.

##### Setup.

Both vanilla and RPG have a linear bonus terms for crossing the $`3.28`$
target loss, $`w\,(3.28-L)`$. NanoGPT requires writing tens of thousands
of tokens in its code. Thus, to ensure efficient training and focus on
making modifications rather than writing executable code, we ask the
agent to read prompt $`s_{t}`$ and propose high-level delta code changes
along with their reasoning for the modification, which is the action
$`a_{t}`$. A separate, independent, frontier model with deterministic
output (zero temperature) serves as the implementer, which reads the
action $`a_{t}`$ proposed by the agent and implements the changes. More
details are in
[Section C.4](#A3.SS4 "C.4 NanoGPT ‣ Appendix C Implementation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").

##### Results.

We present our results on NanoGPT in
[Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In 4.3 Evaluation Results on NanoGPT ‣ 4 Reward-rate for MLE Agent ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents"),
where we observe that RPG gives lower validation loss given the same
time budget than vanilla RL. At the final time budget, we observe that
RPG has an 85.7% margin below $`3.28`$ compared to the baseline. This
can be explained by its objective of using the reward rate, which
intrinsically optimizes for the loss per unit of time. An example of a
self-improvement edit by RPG is shown on the right side of
[Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In 4.3 Evaluation Results on NanoGPT ‣ 4 Reward-rate for MLE Agent ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents"),
where the agent writes a triton kernel, a compiled iteration, and a
learning rate warm-up in its parent script to drive the loss to the
target in less time.

## 5 Related work

##### Machine learning engineering agents.

Many works currently ask whether an agent can carry out machine learning
engineering tasks in an end-to-end fashion ([Nam et al.,
2026](#bib.bib1); [Tang et al., 2023](#bib.bib23); [Chan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib2); [Li et al., 2024](#bib.bib21); [Zhang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib22); [Qiang et al., 2026](#bib.bib4)). Similar lines of
work also include using agents on data science tasks such as data
preprocessing and hyperparameter tuning ([Grosnit et al.,
2024](#bib.bib20); [Bendinelli et al., 2025](#bib.bib19); [Zhang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib18); [Liu et al., 2024](#bib.bib17)). Most agentic
approaches in these tasks involve scaffolding a frozen model, such as by
searching the solution space as a tree ([Jiang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib34)), which do not train MLE-specific experience into the
model weights. One of the closest works to ours is by [Yang et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib15), who trained a small LM with RL on MLE-Bench and
observed that actions take a variable amount of time, but the focus was
on mitigating the time bias favoring faster solutions in asynchronous RL
updates. By contrast, our work directly treats time as a cost term in
the RL objective using the SMDP reward-rate formulation and trains
agents to learn to take efficient actions.

##### Reward-rate RL.

We acknowledge that the reward-rate objective itself is classical. The
SMDP formulation provides the theoretical framework for our method
([Sutton et al., 1999b](#bib.bib24)), and the continuous-time bandit
([György et al., 2007](#bib.bib14)) gives the idea of using off-policy
estimates for the optimal reward rate. Similar problems also appear in
renewal processes with bandit feedback ([Cayci et al.,
2019](#bib.bib13)) where the objective is to maximize reward within a
fixed horizon. A core mathematical toolkit is Dinkelbach iteration for
fractional programming ([Dinkelbach, 1967](#bib.bib7); [Schaible,
1976](#bib.bib6)), where all of these works aforementioned rely on it to
transform a ratio objective into a sequence of linear ones. Budgeted and
knapsack bandits ([Badanidiyuru et al., 2013](#bib.bib16); [Ding et al.,
2013](#bib.bib28); [Xia et al., 2016](#bib.bib27)) also consider actions
with costs, but they enforce a hard constraint on a finite budget. In RL
for LMs literature, the environment is episodic with actions assumed to
have a constant cost ([Schulman et al., 2017](#bib.bib10); [DeepSeek-AI
et al., 2025](#bib.bib11)). A survey on agentic RL with LMs ([Zhang et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib3)) also uses the same formulation, with no notion
of how long an action can take. [Guan et al. (2025)](#bib.bib43) trades
off latency against cost, but requires exploring the Pareto frontier in
a multi-agent framework. To our knowledge, no existing work applies
reward-rate RL in modern LM agents.

##### Self-improvement.

Performing self-improvement by asking an agent to revise its own
previous attempts is a well-established pattern, such as critiquing its
outputs directly ([Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib35)), reflecting on
feedback from the environment ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib36)),
training on the attempts that happened to succeed ([Zelikman et al.,
2022](#bib.bib39)), and rewriting the scaffolding ([Zelikman et al.,
2023](#bib.bib40)). The idea of self-improvement loops has also been
explored in discovery tasks ([Yuksekgonul et al., 2026](#bib.bib25)).
Closer to our setting, the loop can be driven by execution feedback,
where a model repairs its own program from the error message that the
program produced ([Chen et al., 2023](#bib.bib45)). The loop can also be
used on an agent archive to create a tree of diverse and capable agents
through evolutionary search ([Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib46)). [Zeng
et al. (2025)](#bib.bib47) proposes using a balance score for the
exploration-exploitation trade-off and updating models on samples that
are above a score threshold. Our work focuses on using self-improving
loops as state transitions to train agents.

## 6 Conclusion

We proposed a practical reward-rate RL algorithm, namely RPG, for
training efficient MLE agents using the SMDP formulation, where each
action takes variable time, and the objective is long-run reward per
unit of time. RPG uses greedy policy’s reward rate estimates for the
relative reward calculation and directly maximizes it through PPO. It
avoids enumeration over all policies and time-costly on-policy rollouts,
two limitations for directly applying the SMDP methods in practice.
Through theoretical analysis, simulation experiments, and empirical
experiments on MLE-Bench and NanoGPT, we demonstrated that RPG produces
an agent policy that learns to take actions efficiently and maximizes
reward. There are some limitations in this work. The scope of the
empirical experiments is focused on MLE tasks, but other agentic RL
tasks where actions cost variable time exist, so it would be interesting
to see how reward-rate RL does on these tasks. Theoretically, our
analysis focuses on the population-level setting in expectation. A
finite-sample analysis could provide further insight.

### AI Use Statement

In this work, we used generative AI tools for: implement methods,
support qualitative and thematic data analysis, process experiment data,
assist in the writing of proofs, and design or provide feedback on
research methodology or experiments. We have not used generative AI
tools for: generate synthetic data sets, help develop theoretical models
or conceptual frameworks, provide critical ingredients for proving
mathematical claims, formulate mathematical claims, propose or refine
hypotheses, assist with translation, clean and reformat dataset,
interpret results. Additionally, we used generative AI tools for: create
or modify scientific figures or images, create or edit software code,
creation of artifacts, draft parts of a research paper, summarize or
analyse existing literature. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work. We
have checked through all the code edited by AI, and all experiments
involving AI were verified. We take responsibility for the final content
of this work, including text, claims or artifacts produced with the aid
of generative AI.
````
