````math
## Appendix

## Appendix A Derivation

### A.1 Semi-MDP Policy Gradient Theorem

##### Setup and notation.

We consider a finite SMDP ([Sutton et al., 1999b](#bib.bib24); [Das et
al., 1999](#bib.bib12))
$`\mathcal{M}=({\mathcal{S}},{\mathcal{A}},p,\delta_{\min},\delta_{\max})`$
with finite state space $`{\mathcal{S}}`$ and finite action space
$`{\mathcal{A}}`$. At each *decision epoch* the agent observes a state
$`s\in{\mathcal{S}}`$, selects an action $`a\in{\mathcal{A}}`$, and the
environment returns a triple $`(r,\delta,s^{\prime})`$ drawn from the
transition kernel

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p(s^{\prime},r,\delta\mid s,a),\qquad p(s^{\prime}\mid s,a)\;=\;\int\!\!\int p(s^{\prime},r,\delta\mid s,a)\,\mathrm{d}r\mathrm{d}\delta,
``` |  | (12) |

where $`r\in[r_{\min},r_{\max}]`$ is the reward accumulated over the
transition and $`\delta\in[\delta_{\min},\delta_{\max}]`$ is its time
(or duration). We write $`\bar{r}(s,a):=\mathbb{E}[r\mid s,a]`$ and
$`\bar{\delta}(s,a):=\mathbb{E}[\delta\mid s,a]`$ for the conditional
means under
[Equation 12](#A1.E12 "In Setup and notation. ‣ A.1 Semi-MDP Policy Gradient Theorem ‣ Appendix A Derivation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").
Crucially, the kernel does not depend on the policy parameters, so
$`\nabla_{\theta}\bar{r}(s,a)=0`$ and
$`\nabla_{\theta}\bar{\delta}(s,a)=0`$.

Let $`\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)`$ be a differentiable stochastic policy
parameterized by $`\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}`$. We drop the subscript
$`\theta`$ for brevity when clear from context. We abbreviate, for a
fixed policy $`\pi`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bar{\delta}^{\pi}(s)\;:=\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\delta\mid s]\;=\;\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid s)\,\bar{\delta}(s,a).
``` |  | (13) |

Let
$`p^{\pi}(s^{\prime}\mid s):=\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid s)\,p(s^{\prime}\mid s,a)`$
denote the transition matrix of the Markov chain. We write $`d^{\pi}`$
for its unique stationary distribution,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
d^{\pi}(s^{\prime})\;=\;\sum_{s}d^{\pi}(s)\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid s)\,p(s^{\prime}\mid s,a)\qquad\forall\,s^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{S}}.
``` |  | (14) |

We assume that

- •
  $`0<\delta_{\min}\leq\delta\leq\delta_{\max}<\infty`$.
- •
  $`|r|\leq\max\{|r_{\min}|,|r_{\max}|\}<\infty`$.
- •
  $`{\mathcal{S}}`$ and $`{\mathcal{A}}`$ are finite.

Under these assumptions, the long-run *reward rate* (gain per unit time)
of $`\pi`$ is well defined and independent of the initial state:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho(\pi)\;:=\;\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\big[\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}\big]}{\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\big[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\delta_{t}\big]}\;=\;\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[r]}{\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\delta]},\qquad\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\delta]\;:=\;\sum_{s}d^{\pi}(s)\,\bar{\delta}^{\pi}(s),
``` |  | (15) |

with
$`\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[r]:=\sum_{s}d^{\pi}(s)\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid s)\bar{r}(s,a)`$.

The differential state- and action-value functions of $`\pi`$ are

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
V^{\pi}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\big[\,r-\rho(\pi)\delta+V^{\pi}(s^{\prime})\mid s\,\big],\qquad Q^{\pi}(s,a)=\mathbb{E}\big[\,r-\rho(\pi)\delta+V^{\pi}(s^{\prime})\mid s,a\,\big],
``` |  | (16) |

so that $`V^{\pi}(s)=\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid s)Q^{\pi}(s,a)`$.

##### Proof for the policy gradient.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\nabla_{\theta}\,\rho(\pi_{\theta})=\frac{\sum_{s}d^{\pi_{\theta}}(s)\sum_{a}\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)Q^{\pi_{\theta}}(s,a)}{\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}[\delta]},
``` |  | (17) |

where

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
V^{\pi}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\big[r-\rho(\pi)\delta+V^{\pi}(s^{\prime})\mid s\big],\quad Q^{\pi}(s,a)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\big[r-\rho(\pi)\delta+V^{\pi}(s^{\prime})\mid s,a\big].
``` |  |

###### Proof.

For simplicity, we drop $`\theta`$ when clear from context; all
gradients are with respect to $`\theta`$. Differentiating
$`V^{\pi}(s)=\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid s)Q^{\pi}(s,a)`$ and applying the product
rule,

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\nabla V^{\pi}(s)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{a}\Big[\nabla\pi(a\mid s)\,Q^{\pi}(s,a)+\pi(a\mid s)\,\nabla Q^{\pi}(s,a)\Big].`$ |  | (18) |

By definition,
$`Q^{\pi}(s,a)=\bar{r}(s,a)-\rho(\pi)\bar{\delta}(s,a)+\sum_{s^{\prime}}p(s^{\prime}\mid s,a)V^{\pi}(s^{\prime})`$.
Since the transition kernel does not depend on $`\theta`$, we have
$`\nabla\bar{r}(s,a)=0`$ and $`\nabla\bar{\delta}(s,a)=0`$, hence

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\nabla Q^{\pi}(s,a)\;=\;-\,\nabla\rho(\pi)\,\bar{\delta}(s,a)\;+\;\sum_{s^{\prime}}p(s^{\prime}\mid s,a)\,\nabla V^{\pi}(s^{\prime}).
``` |  | (19) |

Substituting
[Equation 19](#A1.E19 "In Proof. ‣ Proof for the policy gradient. ‣ A.1 Semi-MDP Policy Gradient Theorem ‣ Appendix A Derivation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
into
[Equation 18](#A1.E18 "In Proof. ‣ Proof for the policy gradient. ‣ A.1 Semi-MDP Policy Gradient Theorem ‣ Appendix A Derivation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
and using
[Equation 13](#A1.E13 "In Setup and notation. ‣ A.1 Semi-MDP Policy Gradient Theorem ‣ Appendix A Derivation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents"),

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\nabla V^{\pi}(s)=\sum_{a}\Big[\nabla\pi(a\mid s)Q^{\pi}(s,a)+\pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s^{\prime}}p(s^{\prime}\mid s,a)\nabla V^{\pi}(s^{\prime})\Big]\;-\;\nabla\rho(\pi)\,\bar{\delta}^{\pi}(s).
``` |  | (20) |

Multiplying
[Equation 20](#A1.E20 "In Proof. ‣ Proof for the policy gradient. ‣ A.1 Semi-MDP Policy Gradient Theorem ‣ Appendix A Derivation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
by $`d^{\pi}(s)`$ and summing over $`s\in{\mathcal{S}}`$,

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\sum_{s}d^{\pi}(s)\nabla V^{\pi}(s)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{s}d^{\pi}(s)\sum_{a}\nabla\pi(a\mid s)Q^{\pi}(s,a)`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\quad+\underbrace{\sum_{s}d^{\pi}(s)\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s^{\prime}}p(s^{\prime}\mid s,a)\nabla V^{\pi}(s^{\prime})}_{(\star)}\;-\;\nabla\rho(\pi)\sum_{s}d^{\pi}(s)\,\bar{\delta}^{\pi}(s).`$ |  | (21) |

Exchanging the order of summation in $`(\star)`$ and using
[Equation 14](#A1.E14 "In Setup and notation. ‣ A.1 Semi-MDP Policy Gradient Theorem ‣ Appendix A Derivation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
gives,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
(\star)\;=\;\sum_{s^{\prime}}\Big[\sum_{s}d^{\pi}(s)\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid s)p(s^{\prime}\mid s,a)\Big]\nabla V^{\pi}(s^{\prime})\;=\;\sum_{s^{\prime}}d^{\pi}(s^{\prime})\nabla V^{\pi}(s^{\prime}).
``` |  | (22) |

The left-hand side of
[Equation 21](#A1.E21 "In Proof. ‣ Proof for the policy gradient. ‣ A.1 Semi-MDP Policy Gradient Theorem ‣ Appendix A Derivation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
and the term
[Equation 22](#A1.E22 "In Proof. ‣ Proof for the policy gradient. ‣ A.1 Semi-MDP Policy Gradient Theorem ‣ Appendix A Derivation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
are the same finite quantity, they therefore cancel, leaving

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
0\;=\;\sum_{s}d^{\pi}(s)\sum_{a}\nabla\pi(a\mid s)Q^{\pi}(s,a)\;-\;\nabla\rho(\pi)\,\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\delta],
``` |  | (23) |

where we used
$`\sum_{s}d^{\pi}(s)\bar{\delta}^{\pi}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\delta]`$
from
[Equation 15](#A1.E15 "In Setup and notation. ‣ A.1 Semi-MDP Policy Gradient Theorem ‣ Appendix A Derivation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").
Since $`\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\delta]\geq\delta_{\min}>0`$ by the boundeness
assumption, we may divide by it, which completes the proof. ∎

### A.2 More on [György et al. (2007)](#bib.bib14)

We give the explicit form of the two confidence terms $`b_{t}(u)`$ and
$`c_{t}(a,s)`$ appearing in
[Equations 7](#S2.E7 "In 2.2 Continuous Time Bandit ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
and [8](#S2.E8 "Equation 8 ‣ 2.2 Continuous Time Bandit ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
([György et al., 2007](#bib.bib14)).

Let

|     |                                                       |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       T_{u}(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{t}\mathbbm{1}\{a_{j}=u(s_{j})\},
       ```                                                    |     | (24) |

be the number of rounds on which the played action agreed with policy
$`u`$, and

|     |                                                            |     |      |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       T_{a}(s,t)=\sum_{j=1}^{t}\mathbbm{1}\{a_{j}=a,\,s_{j}=s\},
       ```                                                         |     | (25) |

be the number of times action $`a`$ was played in context $`s`$. Both
widths are built from the common scale factor

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\omega_{t,n}\;=\;\sqrt{\frac{\log\big(t\sqrt{|{\mathcal{U}}|+1}\big)}{n}},\qquad|{\mathcal{U}}|=|{\mathcal{A}}|^{|{\mathcal{S}}|}.
``` |  | (26) |

The width on the rate estimate is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
b_{t}(u)\;=\omega_{t,\,T_{u}(t)}\;\sqrt{2\kappa},\qquad\kappa\;=\;2\max\left\{\frac{(r_{\max}-r_{\min})^{2}}{\delta_{\min}^{2}},\;\;\frac{r_{\max}^{2}\,(\delta_{\max}-\delta_{\min})^{2}}{\delta_{\min}^{4}}\right\},
``` |  | (27) |

and the width on the action index is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
c_{t}(a,s)\;=\;(\alpha_{0}+\alpha_{1})\,\omega_{t,\,T_{a}(s,t)},\qquad\alpha_{1}=\delta_{\max}\sqrt{2\kappa},
``` |  | (28) |

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\alpha_{0}=\sqrt{8\max\left\{(r_{\max}-r_{\min})^{2},\;\;\frac{r_{\max}^{2}\,(\delta_{\max}-\delta_{\min})^{2}}{\delta_{\min}^{2}}\right\}}.
``` |  | (29) |

The two widths are indexed differently: $`b_{t}(u)`$ shrinks in the
number of rounds consistent with policy $`u`$, while $`c_{t}(a,s)`$
shrinks in the number of pulls of action $`a`$ in context $`s`$. The
former is subtracted and the latter added, since $`\hat{\rho}_{t}`$
enters
[Equation 8](#S2.E8 "In 2.2 Continuous Time Bandit ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
with a negative sign; pessimism about $`\rho^{*}`$ is optimism about
$`q^{*}`$.

## Appendix B Theoretical Analysis

### B.1 Preliminaries

##### Setup and notation.

We use the same notation as other parts of our paper, which are
discussed in
[Section 2](#S2 "2 Preliminaries ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").
Our setting is same as the bandit setting in
[Section 2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Continuous Time Bandit ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").

##### Reward rate and value.

A stochastic policy $`\pi`$ has reward rate

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho(\pi)\;:=\;\frac{\mathbb{E}_{p}\big[\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid x)\,\bar{r}(x,a)\big]}{\mathbb{E}_{p}\big[\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid x)\,\bar{\delta}(x,a)\big]},\qquad\rho^{*}\;:=\;\max_{u\in{\mathcal{U}}}\rho(u),
``` |  |

where the maximum runs over the deterministic policies
$`{\mathcal{U}}=\{u:{\mathcal{X}}\to{\mathcal{A}}\}`$ of
[Equation 5](#S2.E5 "In 2.2 Continuous Time Bandit ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").
For $`\rho\in\mathbb{R}`$ we define the relative values

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q_{\rho}(x,a)\;:=\;\bar{r}(x,a)-\rho\,\bar{\delta}(x,a),\qquad M_{\rho}(x)\;:=\;\max_{a}q_{\rho}(x,a),\qquad F(\rho)\;:=\;\mathbb{E}_{p}\big[M_{\rho}(x)\big],
``` |  |

with $`q^{*}:=q_{\rho^{*}}`$ and $`a^{*}(x):=\argmax_{a}q^{*}(x,a)`$.

##### Constants.

Since $`r_{\min}\geq 0`$, every policy’s reward rate is in
$`[0,\rho_{\max}]`$, where

|     |                                      |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \rho_{\max}:=r_{\max}/\delta_{\min},
       ```                                   |     |

we define the contraction constant as

|     |                                              |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \chi:=1-\delta_{\min}/\delta_{\max}\in[0,1),
       ```                                           |     |

the time spread²² 2 We assume the expected time for every $`(x,a)`$ pair
cannot be the same since it would reduce the problem into reward
maximization in contextual bandit, thus in the SMDP setting we have
$`\delta_{\mathrm{spr}}\neq 0`$. We do not count it towards our list of
assumptions since it is an intrinsic part of the problem formulation. is

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\delta_{\mathrm{spr}}:=\max_{x}\big[\max_{a}\bar{\delta}(x,a)-\min_{a}\bar{\delta}(x,a)\big]\in(0,\delta_{\max}-\delta_{\min}],
``` |  |

for a rate $`\rho\in\mathbb{R}`$, a greedy policy is denoted as

|     |                                         |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       u_{\rho}(x)\in\argmax_{a}q_{\rho}(x,a),
       ```                                      |     |

thus $`u_{\rho}(x)`$ is a greedy action given reward rate $`\rho`$ in
context $`x`$, under any fixed tie-breaking. Similarly, we define the
greedy margin at $`\rho`$ as

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta(\rho)\;:=\;\min_{x}\big[\max_{a}q_{\rho}(x,a)-\max_{a\neq u_{\rho}(x)}q_{\rho}(x,a)\big],
``` |  |

it is clear that $`\Delta(\rho)\geq 0`$ generally, and
$`\Delta(\rho)>0`$ if and only if the greedy action is unique at every
context $`x`$. With $`\Delta(\rho^{*})`$, we have the gap at the optimal
rate

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta^{*}\;:=\;\Delta(\rho^{*})\;=\;\min_{x}\big[q^{*}(x,a^{*}(x))-\max_{a\neq a^{*}(x)}q^{*}(x,a)\big].
``` |  |

We define the error parameter as
$`\bar{\varepsilon}:=\Delta^{*}/(2\delta_{\mathrm{spr}}),`$ since
$`\delta_{\mathrm{spr}}<\delta_{\max}`$, we have
$`\bar{\varepsilon}>\Delta^{*}/(2\delta_{\max}).`$

##### Algorithm.

The algorithm is softmax policy with NPG, which keeps a conditional
distribution on the actions per context. See
[Section C.1.1](#A3.SS1.SSS1 "C.1.1 Bandit Baselines ‣ C.1 Bandit Experiments ‣ Appendix C Implementation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
for more details.

###### Assumption 1 (A1).

Reward and time are bounded with $`r\in[r_{\min},r_{\max}]`$,
$`\delta\in[\delta_{\min},\delta_{\max}]`$, $`r_{\min}\geq 0`$,
$`\delta_{\min}>0`$.

###### Assumption 2 (A2).

$`\Delta(\rho^{*})=\Delta^{*}>0`$, which is the positive-gap condition
([Auer et al., 2002](#bib.bib26)) for the relative values. Equivalently,
for every $`x`$, the maximizer $`a^{*}(x)`$ of $`q^{*}(x,\cdot)`$ is
unique and the gap between the best and second-best relative value is at
least $`\Delta^{*}`$ at every context.

###### Assumption 3 (A3).

Contexts are i.i.d. from $`p(x)`$, as described in
[Section 2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Continuous Time Bandit ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
and same as in [György et al. (2007)](#bib.bib14).

##### Scope.

Our analysis focuses on the algorithm’s behavior in expectation, i.e.,
$`\hat{Q}_{x,a}(\rho)=q_{\rho}(x,a)`$.

### B.2 Supporting Lemmas

###### Lemma 1.

For $`\rho<\rho^{\prime}`$,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\delta_{\min}\;\leq\;\big(F(\rho)-F(\rho^{\prime})\big)/(\rho^{\prime}-\rho)\;\leq\;\delta_{\max};
``` |  |

in particular $`F`$ is strictly decreasing.

###### Proof.

Let $`\rho<\rho^{\prime}`$, we have

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q_{\rho}(x,a)-q_{\rho^{\prime}}(x,a)=\big(\bar{r}(x,a)-\rho\,\bar{\delta}(x,a)\big)-\big(\bar{r}(x,a)-\rho^{\prime}\,\bar{\delta}(x,a)\big)=(\rho^{\prime}-\rho)\,\bar{\delta}(x,a),
``` |  |

let $`a_{\rho}=\argmax_{a}q_{\rho}(x,a)`$,
$`a_{\rho^{\prime}}=\argmax_{a}q_{\rho^{\prime}}(x,a)`$, then

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
M_{\rho}(x)=q_{\rho}(x,a_{\rho})=q_{\rho^{\prime}}(x,a_{\rho})+(\rho^{\prime}-\rho)\bar{\delta}(x,a_{\rho})\leq M_{\rho^{\prime}}(x)+(\rho^{\prime}-\rho)\delta_{\max},
``` |  |

similarly

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
M_{\rho}(x)\geq q_{\rho}(x,a_{\rho^{\prime}})=q_{\rho^{\prime}}(x,a_{\rho^{\prime}})+(\rho^{\prime}-\rho)\bar{\delta}(x,a_{\rho^{\prime}})\geq M_{\rho^{\prime}}(x)+(\rho^{\prime}-\rho)\delta_{\min}.
``` |  |

Rearrange, and average over every context $`x`$ then gives

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
(\rho^{\prime}-\rho)\delta_{\min}\leq F(\rho)-F(\rho^{\prime})\leq(\rho^{\prime}-\rho)\delta_{\max}.
``` |  |

∎

###### Lemma 2.

$`F(\rho^{*})=0`$, so $`\rho^{*}`$ is the unique root of $`F`$;
$`\rho(\pi)\leq\rho^{*}`$ for every stochastic policy $`\pi`$.

###### Proof.

$`F(\rho^{*})=0`$ can be established by Bellman optimality equation, and
$`F`$ is strictly decreasing, so $`\rho^{*}`$ is unique. For arbitrary
policy $`\pi`$, we have

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\big(\rho(\pi)-\rho^{*}\big)D(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{p}\left[\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid x)q^{*}(x,a)\right]\leq\mathbb{E}_{p}\left[\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid x)M_{\rho^{*}}(x)\right]=F(\rho^{*})=0,
``` |  |

where
$`D(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{p}\left[\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid x)\bar{\delta}(x,a)\right]`$,
thus $`\rho(\pi)\leq\rho^{*}`$. ∎

###### Lemma 3.

Let $`u_{\rho}(x)\in\argmax_{a}q_{\rho}(x,a)`$. If $`\rho\leq\rho^{*}`$,
then $`\rho\leq\rho(u_{\rho})\leq\rho^{*}`$ and

|     |                                                       |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \rho^{*}-\rho(u_{\rho})\;\leq\;\chi\,(\rho^{*}-\rho).
       ```                                                    |     |

###### Proof.

Let $`u_{\rho}(x)=\argmax_{a}q_{\rho}(x,a)`$ be the greedy policy. We
have

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
F(\rho)=\big(\rho(u_{\rho})-\rho\big)D(u_{\rho}),\quad\rho(u_{\rho})=\rho+\frac{F(\rho)}{D(u_{\rho})},
``` |  |

by
[Lemma 1](#Thmlemma1 "Lemma 1. ‣ B.2 Supporting Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents"),
and that $`F(\rho^{*})=0`$, we have

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\delta_{\min}(\rho^{*}-\rho)\leq F(\rho)-F(\rho^{*})=F(\rho)\leq\delta_{\max}(\rho^{*}-\rho),
``` |  |

since $`\rho\leq\rho^{*}`$,
$`F(\rho)\geq\delta_{\min}(\rho^{*}-\rho)\geq 0`$, thus
$`\rho(u_{\rho})\geq\rho`$, and by
[Lemma 2](#Thmlemma2 "Lemma 2. ‣ B.2 Supporting Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents"),
$`\rho\leq\rho(u_{\rho})\leq\rho^{*}`$. For the contraction, we have

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\rho^{*}-\rho(u_{\rho})`$ | $`\displaystyle=(\rho^{*}-\rho)-\frac{F(\rho)}{D(u_{\rho})}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq(\rho^{*}-\rho)-\frac{F(\rho)}{\delta_{\max}}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq(\rho^{*}-\rho)-\frac{\delta_{\min}\,(\rho^{*}-\rho)}{\delta_{\max}}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\Big(1-\frac{\delta_{\min}}{\delta_{\max}}\Big)(\rho^{*}-\rho)=\chi\,(\rho^{*}-\rho).`$ |  |

∎

###### Lemma 4.

For all $`\rho,\rho^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}`$, every $`x`$, and every
$`a\neq u_{\rho^{\prime}}(x)`$,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q_{\rho}\big(x,u_{\rho^{\prime}}(x)\big)-q_{\rho}(x,a)\geq\Delta(\rho^{\prime})-|\rho-\rho^{\prime}|\,\delta_{\mathrm{spr}}.
``` |  |

Consequently
$`\Delta(\rho)\geq\Delta(\rho^{\prime})-|\rho-\rho^{\prime}|\,\delta_{\mathrm{spr}}`$
and hence, by symmetry,
$`|\Delta(\rho)-\Delta(\rho^{\prime})|\leq|\rho-\rho^{\prime}|\,\delta_{\mathrm{spr}}`$:
the greedy margin is $`\delta_{\mathrm{spr}}`$-Lipschitz in the rate. If
moreover
$`|\rho-\rho^{\prime}|\,\delta_{\mathrm{spr}}<\Delta(\rho^{\prime})`$,
then $`u_{\rho}=u_{\rho^{\prime}}`$ point-wise, under any tie-breaking.
Setting $`\rho^{\prime}=\rho^{*}`$ gives,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta(\rho)\geq\Delta^{*}-|\rho-\rho^{*}|\,\delta_{\mathrm{spr}},\qquad\text{and}\qquad u_{\rho}=a^{*}\ \text{ whenever }\ |\rho-\rho^{*}|\,\delta_{\mathrm{spr}}<\Delta^{*},
``` |  |

in particular $`|\rho-\rho^{*}|\leq\bar{\varepsilon}`$ gives
$`u_{\rho}=a^{*}`$ and $`\Delta(\rho)\geq\Delta^{*}/2`$.

###### Proof.

Compare the relative values at two reward-rates $`\rho,\rho^{\prime}`$
similar to
[Lemma 1](#Thmlemma1 "Lemma 1. ‣ B.2 Supporting Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
gives

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q_{\rho}(x,a)=q_{\rho^{\prime}}(x,a)+(\rho^{\prime}-\rho)\bar{\delta}(x,a),\quad\forall x\in{\mathcal{X}},a\in{\mathcal{A}},
``` |  |

denote $`u:=u_{\rho^{\prime}}(x)`$ as the greedy policy, and let
$`a\neq u`$, and substitute the equation above gives

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q_{\rho}(x,u)-q_{\rho}(x,a)=\underbrace{\big[q_{\rho^{\prime}}(x,u)-q_{\rho^{\prime}}(x,a)\big]}_{(1)}+\underbrace{(\rho^{\prime}-\rho)\big[\bar{\delta}(x,u)-\bar{\delta}(x,a)\big]}_{(2)}.
``` |  |

By definition (see
[Section B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Preliminaries ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")),
$`(1)\geq\Delta(\rho^{\prime})`$. For $`(2)`$, both $`\bar{\delta}`$
terms lie within interval
$`[\min_{b}\bar{\delta}(x,b),\max_{b}\bar{\delta}(x,b)]`$, whose length
is at most $`\delta_{\mathrm{spr}}`$
([Section B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Preliminaries ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")),
this gives

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\big|(\rho^{\prime}-\rho)\big[\bar{\delta}(x,u)-\bar{\delta}(x,a)\big]\big|\leq|\rho-\rho^{\prime}|\,\big[\max_{b}\bar{\delta}(x,b)-\min_{b}\bar{\delta}(x,b)\big]\leq|\rho-\rho^{\prime}|\,\delta_{\mathrm{spr}},
``` |  |

which implies

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q_{\rho}(x,u)-q_{\rho}(x,a)\geq\Delta(\rho^{\prime})-|\rho-\rho^{\prime}|\,\delta_{\mathrm{spr}}.
``` |  |

If the right hand side is positive, then it implies that $`u`$ is an
unique maximizer, thus $`u_{\rho^{\prime}}(x)=u_{\rho}(x)`$, then taking
the minimum over $`x`$ gives

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta(\rho)\geq\Delta(\rho^{\prime})-|\rho-\rho^{\prime}|\,\delta_{\mathrm{spr}},
``` |  |

If the right hand side is non-positive, then the above inequality still
holds since $`\Delta(\rho)\geq 0`$ by construction
([Section B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Preliminaries ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")).
By symmetry, we also have that
$`\Delta(\rho^{\prime})\geq\Delta(\rho)-|\rho-\rho^{\prime}|\,\delta_{\mathrm{spr}}`$,
which implies

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
|\Delta(\rho)-\Delta(\rho^{\prime})|\leq|\rho-\rho^{\prime}|\,\delta_{\mathrm{spr}}.
``` |  |

This completes the proof for $`\delta_{\mathrm{spr}}`$-Lipschitz
statement. If
$`|\rho-\rho^{\prime}|\delta_{\mathrm{spr}}<\Delta(\rho^{\prime})`$,
then $`q_{\rho}(x,u)-q_{\rho}(x,a)>0`$, and since
$`u:=u_{\rho^{\prime}}(x)`$, and by uniqueness of the greedy action
assumption
([Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2 (A2). ‣ Algorithm. ‣ B.1 Preliminaries ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")),
we have $`u_{\rho^{\prime}}(x)=u_{\rho}(x)`$ for every $`x`$, i.e., the
greedy policy for the two rates are the same.

For the last statement, substitute $`\rho^{\prime}=\rho^{*}`$ gives the
property

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta(\rho)\geq\Delta^{*}-|\rho-\rho^{*}|\,\delta_{\mathrm{spr}},\qquad\text{and}\qquad u_{\rho}=a^{*}\ \text{ whenever }\ |\rho-\rho^{*}|\,\delta_{\mathrm{spr}}<\Delta^{*},
``` |  |

and with $`\bar{\varepsilon}=\Delta^{*}/(2\delta_{\mathrm{spr}})`$, if
$`|\rho-\rho^{*}|\leq\bar{\varepsilon}`$, then
$`|\rho-\rho^{*}|\delta_{\mathrm{spr}}\leq\Delta^{*}/2<\Delta(\rho^{*})=\Delta^{*}`$,
which implies $`u_{\rho}=a^{*}`$ and $`\Delta(\rho)\geq\Delta^{*}/2`$. ∎

[Lemmas 1](#Thmlemma1 "Lemma 1. ‣ B.2 Supporting Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents"),
[2](#Thmlemma2 "Lemma 2. ‣ B.2 Supporting Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
and [3](#Thmlemma3 "Lemma 3. ‣ B.2 Supporting Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
are statements on the Dinkelbach’s algorithm for fractional programming
similar to those in [Jagannathan (1966)](#bib.bib5); [Dinkelbach
(1967)](#bib.bib7); [Schaible (1976)](#bib.bib6).

### B.3 Main Results

###### Theorem 3.

Let $`\gamma\in[0,1]`$ and $`\rho_{1}\in[0,\rho_{\max}]`$. For every
$`k\geq 1`$, let $`u_{\rho_{k}}(x)\in\argmax_{a}q_{\rho_{k}}(x,a)`$ be a
greedy policy under any tie-breaking and $`\rho(u_{\rho_{k}})`$ is the
reward rate of the greedy policy, let $`\tilde{\rho}_{k+1}`$ be any
value with the sequence satisfying the condition

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{\rho(u_{\rho_{k}})}{1+\gamma}\leq\tilde{\rho}_{k+1}\leq(1+\gamma)\,\rho(u_{\rho_{k}}),\qquad\rho_{k+1}=\mathrm{clip}_{[0,\rho_{\max}]}\big(\tilde{\rho}_{k+1}\big),
``` |  | (30) |

where
$`\mathrm{clip}_{[0,\rho_{\max}]}(z):=\min\{\max\{z,0\},\,\rho_{\max}\}`$.
Then, for every $`k\geq 2`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\left(1-\frac{R\gamma}{1+\gamma}\right)\rho^{*}-\left(\frac{\chi}{1+\gamma}\right)^{k-2}\rho_{\max}\leq\rho_{k}\leq(1+\gamma)\rho^{*},
``` |  | (31) |

where $`R=\delta_{\max}/\delta_{\min}\geq 1`$. If $`\gamma=0`$, then the
sequence increases monotonically
$`\rho_{2}\leq\rho_{3}\leq\cdots\leq\rho^{*}`$ and the iteration reaches
$`\rho_{k}=\rho^{*}`$ after finite steps.

###### Proof.

Throughout the proof, we use the notation

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
N(\pi):=\mathbb{E}_{p}\Big[\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid x)\,\bar{r}(x,a)\Big],\qquad D(\pi):=\mathbb{E}_{p}\Big[\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid x)\,\bar{\delta}(x,a)\Big],
``` |  |

and $`\rho(\pi)=N(\pi)/D(\pi)`$ by definition, and

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{p}\Big[\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid x)\,q_{\rho}(x,a)\Big]`$ | $`\displaystyle=N(\pi)\;-\;\rho\,D(\pi)`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\rho(\pi)\,D(\pi)\;-\;\rho\,D(\pi)=\big(\rho(\pi)-\rho\big)\,D(\pi).`$ |  |

By
[Lemma 1](#Thmlemma1 "Lemma 1. ‣ B.2 Supporting Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents"),
we have

|     |                                                     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       0\leq\rho(u_{\rho_{k}})\leq\rho^{*}\leq\rho_{\max}.
       ```                                                  |     |

We first note that the $`\mathrm{clip}`$ operation survives the upper
and lower bounds. For upper bounds with a nonnegative right hand side:
if $`z\leq B`$ and $`B\geq 0`$, we have

|     |                                                          |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathrm{clip}_{[0,\rho_{\max}]}(z)\leq\max\{z,0\}\leq B,
       ```                                                       |     |

and for lower bounds with a right-hand side at most $`\rho_{\max}`$: if
$`z\geq b`$ with $`b\leq\rho_{\max}`$, then

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{clip}_{[0,\rho_{\max}]}(z)\geq\min\{z,\,\rho_{\max}\}\geq\min\{b,\,\rho_{\max}\}=b.
``` |  |

Since the bounds survive, for notation simplicity, we use $`\rho_{k+1}`$
and $`\tilde{\rho}_{k+1}`$ interchangeably.

For $`k\geq 1`$, using the condition on the sequence in
[Equation 30](#A2.E30 "In Theorem 3. ‣ B.3 Main Results ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents"),
we have

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\tilde{\rho}_{k+1}\leq(1+\gamma)\,\rho(u_{\rho_{k}})\;\leq\;(1+\gamma)\,\rho^{*}\implies\rho_{k+1}\leq(1+\gamma)\rho^{*},
``` |  |

and this completes the upper bound in
[Equation 31](#A2.E31 "In Theorem 3. ‣ B.3 Main Results ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").
To prove the lower bound in
[Equation 31](#A2.E31 "In Theorem 3. ‣ B.3 Main Results ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents"),
we define

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
e_{k}:=\rho^{*}-\rho_{k},\quad B:=\frac{R\gamma\rho^{*}}{1+\gamma}.
``` |  |

To complete the rest of the proof, we enumerate each of the two cases
when $`k\geq 2`$: (i) the below case with $`\rho_{k}\leq\rho^{*}`$. (ii)
the above case with $`\rho^{*}<\rho_{k}\leq(1+\gamma)\rho^{*}`$. For the
below case with $`\rho_{k}\leq\rho^{*}`$, using
[Lemma 3](#Thmlemma3 "Lemma 3. ‣ B.2 Supporting Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
gives

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho(u_{\rho_{k}})\geq\rho^{*}-\chi(\rho^{*}-\rho_{k})=\rho^{*}-\chi e_{k},
``` |  |

using the condition in
[Equation 30](#A2.E30 "In Theorem 3. ‣ B.3 Main Results ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents"),
we have $`\rho_{k+1}\geq\rho(u_{\rho_{k}})/(1+\gamma)`$, which gives

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho^{*}-\rho_{k+1}\leq\rho^{*}-\frac{\rho^{*}-\chi e_{k}}{1+\gamma}=\frac{(1+\gamma)\rho^{*}-\rho^{*}+\chi e_{k}}{1+\gamma}=\frac{\chi e_{k}+\gamma\rho^{*}}{1+\gamma},
``` |  |

thus we established the fact that
$`e_{k+1}\leq\frac{\chi e_{k}+\gamma\rho^{*}}{1+\gamma}`$ for the below
case.

For the above case, $`\rho^{*}<\rho_{k}\leq(1+\gamma)\rho^{*}`$ implies
$`0<\rho_{k}-\rho^{*}\leq\gamma\rho^{*}`$. By
[Lemma 1](#Thmlemma1 "Lemma 1. ‣ B.2 Supporting Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
and the fact that $`\rho^{*}<\rho_{k}`$, we have

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
-\delta_{\max}(\rho_{k}-\rho^{*})\leq F(\rho_{k})\leq-\delta_{\min}(\rho_{k}-\rho^{*})\leq 0.
``` |  | (32) |

Combine together with the fact that
$`F(\rho_{k})/D(u_{\rho_{k}})\geq F(\rho_{k})/\delta_{\min}`$ gives

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{F(\rho_{k})}{D(u_{\rho_{k}})}\geq-\frac{\delta_{\max}}{\delta_{\min}}(\rho_{k}-\rho^{*}),
``` |  | (33) |

which implies

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\rho(u_{\rho_{k}})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\rho_{k}+\frac{F(\rho_{k})}{D(u_{\rho_{k}})}\geq\rho_{k}-\frac{\delta_{\max}}{\delta_{\min}}(\rho_{k}-\rho^{*})`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\rho^{*}+(\rho_{k}-\rho^{*})-\frac{\delta_{\max}}{\delta_{\min}}(\rho_{k}-\rho^{*})`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\rho^{*}-\left(\frac{\delta_{\max}}{\delta_{\min}}-1\right)(\rho_{k}-\rho^{*})\geq\rho^{*}-\left(R-1\right)\gamma\rho^{*},`$ |  |

where the first equality comes from the proof in
[Lemma 3](#Thmlemma3 "Lemma 3. ‣ B.2 Supporting Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").
Use the equation above with the fact
$`\rho_{k+1}\geq\rho(u_{\rho_{k}})/(1+\gamma)`$, we have

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\rho^{*}-\rho_{k+1}`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq\rho^{*}-\frac{\rho(u_{\rho_{k}})}{1+\gamma}`$ |  | (34) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\rho^{*}-\frac{\rho^{*}-(R-1)\gamma\rho^{*}}{1+\gamma}`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\rho^{*}\frac{(1+\gamma)-1+(R-1)\gamma}{1+\gamma}=\frac{R\gamma\rho^{*}}{1+\gamma}=B.`$ |  |  |

Hence we established the fact that $`e_{k+1}\leq B`$ for the above case.
The final proof is to show by induction that the following is true

|     |                                                          |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       e_{k}\leq\tilde{\chi}^{k-2}\rho_{\max}+B,\qquad k\geq 2,
       ```                                                       |     | (35) |

where $`\tilde{\chi}:=\chi/(1+\gamma)\in[0,1)`$. For the base case
$`k=2`$, since $`\rho_{2}\geq 0`$, we have
$`\rho^{*}-\rho_{2}\leq\rho^{*}\leq\rho_{\max}`$, which gives
$`e_{2}\leq\rho_{\max}\leq\rho_{\max}+B`$. For the induction step, we
assume the claim is true for some $`k\geq 2`$ and enumerate each of the
two cases $`\rho_{k}\leq\rho^{*}`$ and $`\rho_{k}>\rho^{*}`$. If
$`\rho_{k}>\rho^{*}`$, then by
[Equation 34](#A2.E34 "In Proof. ‣ B.3 Main Results ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents"),
we have $`e_{k+1}\leq B\leq\tilde{\chi}^{k-1}\rho_{\max}+B`$. If
$`\rho_{k}\leq\rho^{*}`$, then

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle e_{k+1}`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq\frac{\chi e_{k}+\gamma\rho^{*}}{1+\gamma}\leq\frac{\chi\big(\tilde{\chi}^{k-2}\rho_{\max}+B\big)+\gamma\rho^{*}}{1+\gamma}`$ |  | (36) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\tilde{\chi}^{k-1}\rho_{\max}+\frac{\chi B+\gamma\rho^{*}}{1+\gamma},`$ |  |  |

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{\chi B+\gamma\rho^{*}}{1+\gamma}=\frac{\gamma\rho^{*}}{(1+\gamma)^{2}}(\chi R+1+\gamma)\leq\frac{\gamma\rho^{*}}{(1+\gamma)^{2}}(R+R\gamma)=B,
``` |  | (37) |

where the last inequality comes from the identity that $`\chi R+1=R`$,
so $`\chi R+1+\gamma\leq R+R\gamma`$. Combine
[Equation 36](#A2.E36 "In Proof. ‣ B.3 Main Results ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
with
[Equation 37](#A2.E37 "In Proof. ‣ B.3 Main Results ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents"),
we have

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
e_{k+1}\leq\tilde{\chi}^{k-1}\rho_{\max}+\frac{\chi B+\gamma\rho^{*}}{1+\gamma}\leq\tilde{\chi}^{k-1}\rho_{\max}+B,
``` |  |

rearranging the terms gives the lower bound and completes the bound

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho^{*}\left(1-\frac{R\gamma}{1+\gamma}\right)-\left(\frac{\chi}{1+\gamma}\right)^{k-2}\rho_{\max}\leq\rho_{k}.
``` |  |

We now show that when $`\gamma=0`$, then the iteration reaches
$`\rho^{*}`$ in finite steps. If $`\gamma=0`$, we have that every rate
estimate equals to the current greedy policy’s rate
$`\rho_{k+1}=\rho(u_{\rho_{k}})`$, by the identity in
[Equation 33](#A2.E33 "In Proof. ‣ B.3 Main Results ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
and the upper bound $`\rho_{k}\leq\rho^{*}`$ in
[Equation 31](#A2.E31 "In Theorem 3. ‣ B.3 Main Results ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents"),
we have

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho_{k+1}-\rho_{k}=\frac{F(\rho_{k})}{D(u_{\rho_{k}})}\geq\frac{\delta_{\min}}{\delta_{\max}}(\rho^{*}-\rho_{k})\geq 0,
``` |  |

hence the sequence increases monotonically. To prove that it reaches
$`\rho^{*}`$ within finite steps, suppose for sake of contradiction that
$`\{\rho_{k}\}`$ does not reach $`\rho^{*}`$ in finite steps, then we
would have $`\rho_{k}<\rho^{*}`$ for every iteration $`k=2,\cdots,M+2`$,
which implies

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho_{k+1}-\rho_{k}=\frac{F(\rho_{k})}{D(u_{\rho_{k}})}\geq\frac{\delta_{\min}}{\delta_{\max}}(\rho^{*}-\rho_{k})>0,
``` |  |

which means the sequence $`\{\rho_{k}\}`$ is strictly monotonic. Since
greedy policy is a deterministic policy, and there are
$`M=|{\mathcal{A}}|^{|{\mathcal{X}}|}`$ possible deterministic policies,
this means the possible number of reward rate is
$`|\{\rho(u):u\in{\mathcal{U}}\}|\leq M`$. Then we would have
$`\rho_{2}<\rho_{3}<\cdots<\rho_{M+2}`$, which are $`M+1`$ distinct
rates, a contradiction. ∎

###### Proposition 1.

Let $`\bar{\rho}\in\mathbb{R}`$ be any rate with
$`\Delta(\bar{\rho})>0`$, write $`u:=u_{\bar{\rho}}`$ for the greedy
policy at $`\bar{\rho}`$, which is then unique at every context, and run
the algorithm from $`\theta^{(0)}`$ with
$`\pi_{0}:=\pi_{\theta^{(0)}}(u(x)\mid x)`$. For every $`x`$ and
$`k\geq 0`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
1-\pi_{\theta^{(k)}}(u(x)\mid x)\;\leq\;\frac{1-\pi_{0}}{\pi_{0}}\,\exp\big({-\eta\,\Delta(\bar{\rho})\,k}\big),
``` |  | (38) |

in particular
$`1-\pi_{\theta^{(k)}}(u(x)\mid x)\leq(|{\mathcal{A}}|-1)\exp\big({-\eta\,\Delta(\bar{\rho})\,k}\big)`$
when $`\pi_{0}=1/|{\mathcal{A}}|`$ (policy is initially uniform).

###### Proof.

We use same abbreviations as before, where the greedy policy is denoted
as $`u=u_{\hat{\rho}}(x)`$. By definition of the margin, we have

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q_{\bar{\rho}}(x,u)-q_{\bar{\rho}}(x,a)\geq q_{\bar{\rho}}(x,u)-\max_{b\neq u}q_{\bar{\rho}}(x,b)\geq\Delta(\bar{\rho})>0,\qquad\text{for every }a\neq u,
``` |  |

the algorithm updates the logit for each step by

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\theta^{(n+1)}_{x}=\theta^{(n)}_{x}+\eta\Big(q_{\bar{\rho}}(x,\cdot)-\big({\bm{\pi}}^{(n)\top}q_{\bar{\rho}}(x,\cdot)\big)\,{\bm{1}}\Big),
``` |  |

and the logit between actions $`u`$ and $`a`$ is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\theta^{(n+1)}_{x,u}-\theta^{(n+1)}_{x,a}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\Big(\theta^{(n)}_{x,u}+\eta\,q_{\bar{\rho}}(x,u)-\eta\,{\bm{\pi}}^{(n)\top}q_{\bar{\rho}}(x,\cdot)\Big)`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\qquad\ -\Big(\theta^{(n)}_{x,a}+\eta\,q_{\bar{\rho}}(x,a)-\eta\,{\bm{\pi}}^{(n)\top}q_{\bar{\rho}}(x,\cdot)\Big)`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\big(\theta^{(n)}_{x,u}-\theta^{(n)}_{x,a}\big)\;+\;\eta\big(q_{\bar{\rho}}(x,u)-q_{\bar{\rho}}(x,a)\big),`$ |  |

write $`d^{(n)}:=\theta^{(n)}_{x,u}-\theta^{(n)}_{x,a}`$ for the logit
gap and $`c\;:=\;\eta\big(q_{\bar{\rho}}(x,u)-q_{\bar{\rho}}(x,a)\big)`$
for the update gap, the parameter update rule thus becomes a recursion
of the form $`d^{(n+1)}=d^{(n)}+c`$. Writing as a telescoping sum over
$`n=0,\ldots,k-1`$ gives

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
d^{(k)}-d^{(0)}=\sum_{n=0}^{k-1}\big(d^{(n+1)}-d^{(n)}\big)=\sum_{n=0}^{k-1}c\;=\;k\,c,
``` |  |

thus we have

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\theta^{(k)}_{x,u}-\theta^{(k)}_{x,a}=\theta^{(0)}_{x,u}-\theta^{(0)}_{x,a}+\eta\,k\big(q_{\bar{\rho}}(x,u)-q_{\bar{\rho}}(x,a)\big),
``` |  |

since our distribution is parameterized through softmax, we have

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a\mid x)}{\pi_{\theta}(u\mid x)}=\frac{\exp(\theta_{x,a})/\sum_{b}\exp(\theta_{x,b})}{\exp(\theta_{x,u})/\sum_{b}\exp(\theta_{x,b})}=\exp(\theta_{x,a}-\theta_{x,u}),
``` |  |

fix $`a\neq u`$, and apply the two equations together, we have

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\frac{\pi_{\theta^{(k)}}(a\mid x)}{\pi_{\theta^{(k)}}(u\mid x)}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\exp\big(\theta^{(k)}_{x,a}-\theta^{(k)}_{x,u}\big)`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\exp\Big(\theta^{(0)}_{x,a}-\theta^{(0)}_{x,u}-\eta\,k\big(q_{\bar{\rho}}(x,u)-q_{\bar{\rho}}(x,a)\big)\Big)`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\pi_{\theta^{(0)}}(a\mid x)}{\pi_{\theta^{(0)}}(u\mid x)}\;\exp\Big({-\eta\,k\big(q_{\bar{\rho}}(x,u)-q_{\bar{\rho}}(x,a)\big)}\Big),`$ |  |

observe that

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
-\eta\,k\big(q_{\bar{\rho}}(x,u)-q_{\bar{\rho}}(x,a)\big)\;\leq\;-\eta\,k\,\Delta(\bar{\rho}),
``` |  |

thus

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{\pi_{\theta^{(k)}}(a\mid x)}{\pi_{\theta^{(k)}}(u\mid x)}\;\leq\;\frac{\pi_{\theta^{(0)}}(a\mid x)}{\pi_{\theta^{(0)}}(u\mid x)}\;\exp({-\eta\Delta(\bar{\rho})k}),
``` |  |

taking the sum over all $`a\neq u`$ gives the following for the left
hand side

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\sum_{a\neq u}\frac{\pi_{\theta^{(k)}}(a\mid x)}{\pi_{\theta^{(k)}}(u\mid x)}=\frac{\sum_{a\neq u}\pi_{\theta^{(k)}}(a\mid x)}{\pi_{\theta^{(k)}}(u\mid x)}=\frac{1-\pi_{\theta^{(k)}}(u\mid x)}{\pi_{\theta^{(k)}}(u\mid x)},
``` |  |

and the following for the right hand side

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\sum_{a\neq u}\frac{\pi_{\theta^{(0)}}(a\mid x)}{\pi_{\theta^{(0)}}(u\mid x)}\;\exp({-\eta\Delta(\bar{\rho})k})=\frac{1-\pi_{0}}{\pi_{0}}\;\exp({-\eta\Delta(\bar{\rho})k}),
``` |  |

together we have

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{1-\pi_{\theta^{(k)}}(u\mid x)}{\pi_{\theta^{(k)}}(u\mid x)}\;\leq\;\frac{1-\pi_{0}}{\pi_{0}}\;\exp({-\eta\Delta(\bar{\rho})k}),
``` |  |

multiplying both sides by $`\pi_{\theta^{(k)}}(u\mid x)`$ gives

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle 1-\pi_{\theta^{(k)}}(u\mid x)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\pi_{\theta^{(k)}}(u\mid x)\;\frac{1-\pi_{\theta^{(k)}}(u\mid x)}{\pi_{\theta^{(k)}}(u\mid x)}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\pi_{\theta^{(k)}}(u\mid x)\;\frac{1-\pi_{0}}{\pi_{0}}\;\exp({-\eta\Delta(\bar{\rho})k})`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\frac{1-\pi_{0}}{\pi_{0}}\;\exp({-\eta\Delta(\bar{\rho})k}),`$ |  |

and hence completes the proof. ∎

###### Corollary 1.

Let $`\bar{\rho}\in\mathbb{R}`$ be any rate with smallness condition
$`|\bar{\rho}-\rho^{*}|\leq\bar{\varepsilon}`$,
$`\bar{\varepsilon}=\Delta^{*}/(2\delta_{\mathrm{spr}})`$. Then
$`u_{\bar{\rho}}=a^{*}`$, for every $`x`$, $`a\neq a^{*}(x)`$,
$`k\geq 0`$

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
1-\pi_{\theta^{(k)}}(a^{*}(x)\mid x)\leq\frac{1-\pi_{0}}{\pi_{0}}\,\exp\big({-\eta\,\Delta^{*}k/2}\big),
``` |  | (39) |

in particular
$`1-\pi_{\theta^{(k)}}(a^{*}(x)\mid x)\leq(|{\mathcal{A}}|-1)\exp({-\eta\Delta^{*}k/2})`$
at the zero initialization.

###### Proof.

Apply
[Lemma 4](#Thmlemma4 "Lemma 4. ‣ B.2 Supporting Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
with
[Proposition 1](#Thmproposition1 "Proposition 1. ‣ B.3 Main Results ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").
∎

###### Theorem 4.

Let $`\rho_{1},\rho_{2},\ldots`$ be a sequence of reward rates. Denote
$`\theta^{(k)}`$ as the parameter for the softmax logit after $`k`$
steps from the zero initialization and
$`\bar{\rho}_{k}=\sum_{n\leq k}\rho_{n}/k`$, then for every $`x`$,
$`k\geq 1`$, the policy $`\pi^{(k)}`$ is a Boltzmann policy of
$`q_{\bar{\rho}_{k}}(x,a)`$ with inverse temperature $`\eta k`$, and if
$`\rho_{k+1}=\rho(u_{\bar{\rho}_{k}})`$, $`\rho_{1}\in[0,\rho^{*}]`$,
then

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho^{*}-\bar{\rho}_{k}\;\leq\;(\rho^{*}-\bar{\rho}_{1})\,\exp(1-\chi)\,(k+1)^{-(1-\chi)},
``` |  | (40) |

thus $`\bar{\rho}_{k}`$ converges to $`\rho^{*}`$ at
$`O(k^{-(1-\chi)})`$. Moreover, for every

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
k\;\geq\;k_{0}\;:=\;\Big\lceil\big(\exp(1-\chi)\,(\rho^{*}-\bar{\rho}_{1})/\bar{\varepsilon}\big)^{1/(1-\chi)}\Big\rceil,
``` |  | (41) |

the greedy policy at the running average is optimal,
$`u_{\bar{\rho}_{k}}=a^{*}`$ point-wise, and for every $`x`$

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
1-\pi^{(k)}(a^{*}(x)\mid x)\;\leq\;(|{\mathcal{A}}|-1)\,\exp\big({-\eta\,\Delta^{*}k/2}\big).
``` |  | (42) |

###### Proof.

Observe that the relative value $`q_{\rho_{n}}(x,a)`$ for action $`a`$
and context $`x`$ at step $`n`$ can be expressed as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\sum_{n\leq k}q_{\rho_{n}}(x,a)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{n\leq k}\big(\bar{r}(x,a)-\rho_{n}\,\bar{\delta}(x,a)\big)\;=\;k\,\bar{r}(x,a)\;-\;\Big(\sum_{n\leq k}\rho_{n}\Big)\bar{\delta}(x,a)`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=k\,\big(\bar{r}(x,a)-\bar{\rho}_{k}\,\bar{\delta}(x,a)\big)=k\,q_{\bar{\rho}_{k}}(x,a),`$ |  |

By the parameter update rule for NPG with a softmax policy
$`\theta^{\prime}_{x}=\theta_{x}+\eta(q-\langle{\bm{\pi}},q\rangle{\bm{1}})`$,
fix the context, and expand the terms through the recursion gives

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\theta^{(k)}_{x}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\eta\sum_{n\leq k}q_{\rho_{n}}(x,\cdot)\;-\;\eta\Bigg(\sum_{n\leq k}s_{n}\Bigg){\bm{1}}\qquad s_{n}:=\big\langle{\bm{\pi}}^{(n-1)},q_{\rho_{n}}(x,\cdot)\big\rangle`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\eta\,k\,q_{\bar{\rho}_{k}}(x,\cdot)\;+\;c_{k}(x)\,{\bm{1}}\qquad c_{k}(x):=-\eta\sum_{n\leq k}s_{n},`$ |  |

when the logit $`\theta_{x}^{(k)}`$ is feed into the softmax function,
since softmax is invariant to addition of constants, the $`c_{k}(x)`$
term is ignored, thus the policy becomes the Boltzmann policy of
$`\eta\,k\,q_{\bar{\rho}_{k}}(x,a)`$ and completes the first part of the
proof. For the second part, first define the estimated rate as
$`k\bar{\rho}_{k}=\sum_{n\leq k}\rho_{n}`$, then

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bar{\rho}_{k+1}=\frac{1}{k+1}\sum_{n\leq k+1}\rho_{n}=\frac{k\,\bar{\rho}_{k}+\rho_{k+1}}{k+1}=\frac{k}{k+1}\,\bar{\rho}_{k}\;+\;\frac{1}{k+1}\,\rho_{k+1},
``` |  |

which is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bar{\rho}_{k+1}=(1-\alpha_{k})\bar{\rho}_{k}+\alpha_{k}\,\rho_{k+1},\qquad\alpha_{k}=1/(k+1).
``` |  | (43) |

Since the algorithm only accepts samples selected by
$`\argmax_{a}\theta_{x,a}`$, we assume that the rate estimate equals to
the greedy policy’s rate under $`\bar{\rho}_{k}`$, i.e.,
$`\rho_{k+1}=\rho(u_{\bar{\rho}_{k}})`$. Since
$`\bar{\rho}_{k}\leq\rho^{*}`$ at $`k=1`$ by assumption,
[Lemma 3](#Thmlemma3 "Lemma 3. ‣ B.2 Supporting Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
gives that $`\rho(u_{\bar{\rho}_{k}})\geq\bar{\rho}_{k}`$ and
$`\rho^{*}-\rho(u_{\bar{\rho}_{k}})\leq\chi(\rho^{*}-\bar{\rho}_{k})`$.
$`\bar{\rho}_{k+1}`$ is a convex combination of $`\bar{\rho}_{k}`$ and
$`\rho(u_{\bar{\rho}_{k}})`$ by
[Equation 43](#A2.E43 "In Proof. ‣ B.3 Main Results ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
and we have $`\bar{\rho}_{k}\leq\bar{\rho}_{k+1}\leq\rho^{*}`$.
Subtracting
[Equation 43](#A2.E43 "In Proof. ‣ B.3 Main Results ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
from $`\rho^{*}`$ gives

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\rho^{*}-\bar{\rho}_{k+1}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\rho^{*}+\alpha_{k}\rho^{*}-\alpha_{k}\rho^{*}-(1-\alpha_{k})\bar{\rho}_{k}-\alpha_{k}\rho_{k+1}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=(1-\alpha_{k})(\rho^{*}-\bar{\rho}_{k})+\alpha_{k}(\rho^{*}-\rho_{k+1})`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq(1-\alpha_{k})(\rho^{*}-\bar{\rho}_{k})+\alpha_{k}\chi(\rho^{*}-\bar{\rho}_{k})=\big(1-\alpha_{k}(1-\chi)\big)(\rho^{*}-\bar{\rho}_{k}).`$ |  |

Denote $`e_{k}=\rho^{*}-\bar{\rho}_{k}`$,
$`c:=1-\chi=\delta_{\min}/\delta_{\max}\in(0,1]`$, and expand the
recursion gives

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle e_{k}`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq e_{1}\prod_{m=2}^{k}\big(1-c/m\big)\leq e_{1}\exp\left({-c\sum_{m=2}^{k}1/m}\right)`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq e_{1}\exp\big(c-c\log(k+1)\big)=e_{1}\exp(c)\,(k+1)^{-c},`$ |  |

where we used the fact $`1-z\leq\exp(-z)`$ and
$`\sum_{m\leq k}1/m\geq\log(k+1)`$.

Since $`\rho_{k+1}=\rho(u_{\bar{\rho}_{k}})\leq\rho^{*}`$,
$`\bar{\rho}_{k+1}\leq(1-\alpha_{k})\bar{\rho}_{k}+\alpha_{k}\rho^{*}<\rho^{*}`$
whenever $`\bar{\rho}_{k}<\rho^{*}`$, so by induction
$`\rho_{1}<\rho^{*}`$ keeps the strict inequality
$`\bar{\rho}_{k}<\rho^{*}`$ to every $`k>1`$.

For the last part, the second part gives
$`\bar{\rho}_{k}\leq\bar{\rho}_{k+1}\leq\rho^{*}`$, so the error
$`\rho^{*}-\bar{\rho}_{k}`$ is non-increasing in $`k`$ and it suffices
to find the first index at which it falls below $`\bar{\varepsilon}`$.
By
[Equation 40](#A2.E40 "In Theorem 4. ‣ B.3 Main Results ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents"),
$`\rho^{*}-\bar{\rho}_{k}\leq\bar{\varepsilon}`$ holds when

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
(k+1)^{1-\chi}\geq\exp(1-\chi)\,(\rho^{*}-\bar{\rho}_{1})/\bar{\varepsilon},
``` |  |

thus we need

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
k\geq\big(\exp(1-\chi)\,(\rho^{*}-\bar{\rho}_{1})/\bar{\varepsilon}\big)^{1/(1-\chi)}-1,
``` |  |

thus we can set $`k_{0}`$ to be the constant stated in
[Equation 41](#A2.E41 "In Theorem 4. ‣ B.3 Main Results ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents"),
and it then holds at every subsequent step $`k\geq k_{0}`$. When
$`k\geq k_{0}`$, since
$`|\bar{\rho}_{k}-\rho^{*}|\leq\bar{\varepsilon}`$, we can apply
[Lemma 4](#Thmlemma4 "Lemma 4. ‣ B.2 Supporting Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents"),
which gives $`u_{\bar{\rho}_{k}}=u_{\rho^{*}}=a^{*}`$ and
$`\Delta(\bar{\rho}_{k})\geq\Delta^{*}/2`$. Similar to the steps in the
proofs for
[Propositions 1](#Thmproposition1 "Proposition 1. ‣ B.3 Main Results ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
and [1](#Thmcorollary1 "Corollary 1. ‣ B.3 Main Results ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents"),
the probability ratio is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\frac{\pi^{(k)}(a\mid x)}{\pi^{(k)}(a^{*}(x)\mid x)}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\exp\Big({-\eta\,k\big(q_{\bar{\rho}_{k}}(x,a^{*}(x))-q_{\bar{\rho}_{k}}(x,a)\big)}\Big)`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\exp\big({-\eta\,k\,\Delta(\bar{\rho}_{k})}\big)`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\exp\big({-\eta\,\Delta^{*}\,k/2}\big),`$ |  |

sum over all actions $`a\neq a^{*}(x)`$ gives

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{1-\pi^{(k)}(a^{*}(x)\mid x)}{\pi^{(k)}(a^{*}(x)\mid x)}\leq(|{\mathcal{A}}|-1)\exp\big({-\eta\,\Delta^{*}\,k/2}\big),
``` |  |

which gives
[Equation 42](#A2.E42 "In Theorem 4. ‣ B.3 Main Results ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
after multiplying both sides by $`\pi^{(k)}(a^{*}(x)\mid x)\leq 1`$ and
completes the proof. ∎

## Appendix C Implementation

### C.1 Bandit Experiments

This section gives the full specification of the bandit experiments in
[Section 3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Bandit Validation ‣ 3 Reward-rate Policy Gradient ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").

#### C.1.1 Bandit Baselines

##### C-UCB with theoretical constants.

The algorithm of [György et al. (2007)](#bib.bib14), implemented
faithfully for all the constants.

##### C-UCB with tuned constants.

Identical in every respect, except that the two scale constants of
[Equations 27](#A1.E27 "In A.2 More on ( ) ‣ Appendix A Derivation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
and [28](#A1.E28 "Equation 28 ‣ A.2 More on ( ) ‣ Appendix A Derivation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
are replaced by free parameters $`c_{1}`$ and $`c_{2}`$ selected via
grid search.

##### C-UCB with approximation.

C-UCB involves enumeration over all policies for reward-rate estimation.
This is infeasible when we have many arms and contexts. As an
approximation, we draw 2048 policies uniformly random from policies
constructed from visited arms and contexts, and enumerate on these 2048
policies.

##### NPG.

The reward-rate learner keeps one independent softmax head per context:
a tabular parameter matrix
$`\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{|{\mathcal{X}}|\times(K+1)}`$ with one free logit
per $`(x,a)`$ pair, initialized to zero so that
$`\pi_{\theta}(a\mid x)=1/(K+1)`$ is uniform, and

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\pi_{\theta}(a\mid x)\;=\;\frac{\exp(\theta_{x,a})}{\sum_{b}\exp(\theta_{x,b})}.
``` |  | (44) |

At each round the learner observes $`x`$, samples
$`a\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)`$, and receives $`(r,\delta)`$, and its
regret is incurred by its own action choices. The update rule is the
natural gradient of the relative reward

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\theta_{x}\leftarrow\theta_{x}+\eta\,{\bm{z}},\quad\nabla_{\theta_{x}}\,J(\theta)={\mathbf{F}}(\theta_{x}){\bm{z}},
``` |  | (45) |

where the Fisher information matrix $`{\mathbf{F}}`$ is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
{\mathbf{F}}(\theta_{x})=\mathrm{diag}({\bm{\pi}})-{\bm{\pi}}{\bm{\pi}}^{\top},
``` |  | (46) |

which simplifies to adding the advantage to the logits directly. Writing
$`{\bm{\pi}}=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)`$, $`{\bm{s}}`$ for the vector
with entries $`s_{a}=\mathbb{E}[\,r-\rho^{*}\delta\mid x,a\,]`$,
$`J={\bm{\pi}}^{\!\top}{\bm{s}}`$ and
$`{\bm{a}}={\bm{s}}-\big({\bm{\pi}}^{\!\top}{\bm{s}}\big){\bm{1}}`$ be
the advantages

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\frac{\partial\pi_{a}}{\partial\theta_{c}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\pi_{a}\big(\mathbbm{1}\{a=c\}-\pi_{c}\big)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\nabla_{\theta_{x}}J={\bm{\pi}}\odot{\bm{a}},`$ |  | (47) |

solving for $`{\mathbf{F}}{\bm{z}}={\bm{\pi}}\odot{\bm{a}}`$ gives
$`{\bm{z}}={\bm{a}}`$ as one of the solutions, thus the update rule is

|     |                                                           |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \theta_{x}\leftarrow\theta_{x}+\eta\,A_{\theta}(x,\cdot).
       ```                                                        |     |

The advantage is needed for every arm while a bandit learner observes
only the arm it played, so we keep a per-cell buffer of the raw sums
$`S^{r}_{x,a}`$ and $`S^{\delta}_{x,a}`$ with counts $`n_{x,a}`$, and
use them to estimate the expected relative reward under current
estimated rate $`\hat{\rho}_{t}`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widehat{Q}_{x,a}\;=\;\begin{cases}\big(S^{r}_{x,a}-\hat{\rho}_{t}\,S^{\delta}_{x,a}\big)/n_{x,a},&n_{x,a}>0,\\[2.0pt]
0,&n_{x,a}=0,\end{cases}\qquad\theta_{x}\;\leftarrow\;\theta_{x}+\eta\big(\widehat{Q}_{x}-({\bm{\pi}}^{\!\top}\widehat{Q}_{x}){\bm{1}}\big).
``` |  | (48) |

The rate $`\hat{\rho}_{t}`$ is supplied by the online NIW estimator.

##### Vanilla policy gradient.

Everything is kept same as NPG, except the gradient update is

|     |                                                                  |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \theta_{x}\leftarrow\theta_{x}+\eta\nabla_{\theta_{x}}J(\theta),
       ```                                                               |     |

which gives the update rule

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\theta_{x}\leftarrow\theta_{x}+\eta\;{\bm{\pi}}\odot\big(\hat{Q}_{x}-({\bm{\pi}}^{\top}\hat{Q}_{x}){\bm{1}}\big).
``` |  |

##### The NIW rate estimator.

The estimate $`\hat{\rho}_{t}`$ is fitted online on pairs of accumulated
reward and accumulated time, mirroring the way the rate is formed from
per-slot accumulators in MLE-Bench and NanoGPT
([Section 4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Instantiating Language Models for Reward-rate Policies ‣ 4 Reward-rate for MLE Agent ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")).
It is refitted every $`8`$ steps, and $`\hat{\rho}_{t}`$ is the 95th
percentile among posterior-predictive samples (see
[Section C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Reward-rate Predictor ‣ Appendix C Implementation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")).
The accumulators are *gated*, in that a sample enters an accumulator
only when the arm played was the current $`\argmax_{a}\,\theta_{a,x}`$,
so that the estimate describes the greedy policy. They are also
*age-bounded*, in that a slot restarts once it is older than $`A`$
steps, with $`A`$ tuned with hyperparameter search. We note that this
estimator does not guarantee exact estimation of the greedy policy’s
reward rate. Rather, it serves as a test case to see how our algorithm
behaves when the greedy reward rate has approximation error, which is
the case in empirical settings.

#### C.1.2 Experiment Setup

##### Setup.

At each decision epoch the learner selects an action $`a`$ and observes
a reward $`r\geq 0`$ together with a time $`\delta>0`$. The pair is
drawn jointly, so the reward and the time it costs may be dependent.
Performance is measured against the optimal reward rate $`\rho^{*}`$,
and we report the realized regret of
[Equation 6](#S2.E6 "In 2.2 Continuous Time Bandit ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
at step $`t`$. Each context and action pair consists of a mean reward
and time parameter, forming a table of size $`(K,|{\mathcal{X}}|)`$. The
setup for these mean parameters are described below. To ensure we do not
introduce bias in terms of ordering of the arms and contexts, we perform
a permutation on $`K`$ arm indices and $`|{\mathcal{X}}|`$ context
indices for every trial.

##### Arm design.

The $`K+1`$ actions available in a context are the skip action and two
structurally different kinds of arm, which are specified in opposite
directions. The four designed arms fix the pair
$`(\mathbb{E}[r(a)],\mathbb{E}[\delta(a)])`$ and let the rate follow:

- •
  best arm $`(0.50,1.0)`$ at rate $`0.500`$.
- •
  decoy $`(0.57,1.2)`$ at rate $`0.475`$, carrying higher raw reward at
  a $`5\%`$ relative rate deficit.
- •
  trap $`(0.90,3.0)`$ at rate $`0.300`$, the highest raw reward in the
  context at the worst rate.
- •
  fast arm $`(0.21,0.6)`$ at rate $`0.350`$ that is cheap but weak.

The decoy and the trap both exist to punish an agent that maximizes
reward rather than reward per unit of time. The remaining $`K-4`$ filler
arms fix the rate and derive the reward and time from it

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\begin{gathered}\zeta_{j}=\beta_{x}\Big(0.42-\tfrac{j}{K-5}\big(0.42-0.18\big)\Big),\quad\mathbb{E}[\delta(4+j)]=d_{j},\\
d_{j}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0.70,\,2.00),\quad\mathbb{E}[r(4+j)]=\zeta_{j}\,d_{j},\end{gathered}
``` |  | (49) |

for $`j=0,\dots,K-5`$, where $`\beta_{x}`$ is the reward scale of the
context (see below) and each $`d_{j}`$ is drawn independently. This
means the reward rate is monotone but reward and time are unordered, so
neither quantity on its own identifies a good arm. No filler arm is ever
optimal, because the sequence’s maximum is at $`0.42\,\beta_{x}`$,
strictly below the best arm at $`0.50\,\beta_{x}`$. Filler arms
therefore widen the action set at controlled rate spacing rather than
competing for the optimum, which makes $`K`$ an exploration-difficulty
axis.

##### Context Design.

A context $`x\in{\mathcal{X}}`$ is drawn uniformly at each epoch and
adds a skip action with $`(0,0.35)`$. A context is summarized by the
reward scale $`\beta_{x}`$, which multiplies every reward and leaves
time untouched; since the rate is reward divided by time, $`\beta_{x}`$
scales the rate as well. Four contexts are designed:

- •
  marginal ($`\beta_{x}=1.00`$) reproduces the arm design above and
  serves as the baseline.
- •
  rich ($`\beta_{x}=1.50`$) holds the highest multiplier.
- •
  poor ($`\beta_{x}=0.32`$) so that skip can be considered.
- •
  coupling is not a rescaling at all. Instead, it replaces the four
  designed arms with $`(1.80,2.00)`$, $`(1.00,1.00)`$, $`(1.60,3.0)`$
  and $`(0.20,0.6)`$, a slow-but-rich arm at rate $`0.90`$ against a
  fast-but-lean arm at rate $`1.00`$.

Maximizing the rate within coupling takes the fast arm while the optimal
policy takes the slow one, which is why the problem does not decompose
into $`|{\mathcal{X}}|`$ independent bandits. This property holds as
long as $`\rho^{*}<0.8`$, which is the case for all of our simulations.
Any context beyond these four is filler, where $`\beta_{x}`$’s are
uniformly binned midpoints between $`[0.42,1.35]`$, the range between
poor and rich.

##### Environment families.

Four families vary the dependence between reward and time while holding
the marginal means fixed. Let $`\mu^{r}_{a}=\mathbb{E}[r_{a}]`$ and
$`\mu^{\delta}_{a}=\mathbb{E}[\delta_{a}]`$ be the designed means of arm
$`a`$. We fix $`\sigma_{r}=0.20`$, a time noise fraction
$`\varsigma=0.15`$, a log-scale spread $`\sigma_{\log}=0.5`$, and a time
floor $`\delta_{\min}=0.5`$. Every family draws a pair of standard
normals $`z_{1},\xi\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,1)`$ and couples them through a
Gaussian copula

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
z_{2}\;=\;\varrho\,z_{1}\;+\;\sqrt{1-\varrho^{2}}\;\xi,\qquad\mathrm{corr}(z_{1},z_{2})=\varrho,
``` |  | (50) |

so that $`\varrho`$ alone controls the reward–time dependence while both
marginals are unchanged.

E1 (independent), $`\varrho=0`$. Reward and time are rectified normals
drawn independently,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r_{a}=\max\big(\mu^{r}_{a}+\sigma_{r}z_{1},0\big),\qquad\delta_{a}=\max\big(\mu^{\delta}_{a}+\varsigma\,\mu^{\delta}_{a}z_{2},\;\delta_{\min}\big).
``` |  | (51) |

E2 (positively coupled), $`\varrho=+0.8`$ and E3 (negatively coupled),
$`\varrho=-0.8`$. Identical marginals to
[Equation 51](#A3.E51 "In Environment families. ‣ C.1.2 Experiment Setup ‣ C.1 Bandit Experiments ‣ Appendix C Implementation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents"),
with $`z_{2}`$ generated by
[Equation 50](#A3.E50 "In Environment families. ‣ C.1.2 Experiment Setup ‣ C.1 Bandit Experiments ‣ Appendix C Implementation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").
Under E2 a high-reward draw tends to also be slow, so the empirical rate
$`r/\delta`$ is compressed and a learner that ranks arms by raw reward
is punished less; under E3 high reward tends to arrive fast, which
inflates the apparent spread in rates.

E4 (lognormal), $`\varrho=+0.5`$ on the log scale. Both coordinates are
lognormal with heavy right tails. Note that we take the log on the mean
parameter so that the expectation
$`\mathbb{E}[r_{a}],\mathbb{E}[\delta_{a}]`$ still equals to
$`\mu^{r}_{a},\mu^{\delta}_{a}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r_{a}=\exp\!\Big(\log\mu^{r}_{a}-\tfrac{\sigma_{\log}^{2}}{2}+\sigma_{\log}z_{1}\Big),\qquad\delta_{a}=\max\!\Big(\exp\!\big(\log\mu^{\delta}_{a}-\tfrac{\sigma_{\log}^{2}}{2}+\sigma_{\log}z_{2}\big),\;\delta_{\min}\Big).
``` |  | (52) |

The rectification and the floor $`\delta_{\min}`$ make the realized
marginals differ slightly from $`(\mu^{r}_{a},\mu^{\delta}_{a})`$, so we
do not rely on the design values when computing $`\rho^{*}`$ (See
[Equation 58](#A3.E58 "In Ground truth. ‣ C.1.2 Experiment Setup ‣ C.1 Bandit Experiments ‣ Appendix C Implementation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")).
Every reported mean is instead computed in closed form, using

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}[\max(X,c)]=c\,\Phi(a)+m\big(1-\Phi(a)\big)+s\,\phi(a),\quad a=\tfrac{c-m}{s},
``` |  | (53) |

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}[\max(Y,c)]=c\,\Phi(b)+m\big(1-\Phi(b-\sigma_{\log})\big),\quad b=\tfrac{\log c-\mu}{\sigma_{\log}},
``` |  | (54) |

for a rectified normal $`X\sim{\mathcal{N}}(m,s^{2})`$ and a floored
lognormal $`Y`$ with log-scale $`\sigma_{\log}`$. $`\phi,\Phi`$ are PDF
and CDF of Gaussian, respectively. The means are therefore deterministic
and do not require Monte Carlo approximation, and $`\rho^{*}`$ follows
from
[Equation 58](#A3.E58 "In Ground truth. ‣ C.1.2 Experiment Setup ‣ C.1 Bandit Experiments ‣ Appendix C Implementation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").

##### Ground truth.

The general average-reward SMDP optimality equation reads

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
V^{*}(x)=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\Big\{\mathbb{E}[r(x,a)]-\rho^{*}\,\mathbb{E}[\delta(x,a)]+\sum_{x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}}p(x^{\prime}\mid x,a)\,V^{*}(x^{\prime})\Big\}.
``` |  | (55) |

In the bandit case the next context is drawn independently of the
current context and of the action taken, so
$`p(x^{\prime}\mid x,a)=p(x^{\prime})`$ and the continuation term
collapses to a constant
$`c:=\sum_{x^{\prime}}p(x^{\prime})V^{*}(x^{\prime})`$ that depends on
neither $`x`$ nor $`a`$. Writing

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q^{*}(x,a):=\mathbb{E}[r(x,a)]-\rho^{*}\,\mathbb{E}[\delta(x,a)],
``` |  | (56) |

[Equation 55](#A3.E55 "In Ground truth. ‣ C.1.2 Experiment Setup ‣ C.1 Bandit Experiments ‣ Appendix C Implementation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
becomes

|     |                                              |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       V^{*}(x)=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}q^{*}(x,a)+c.
       ```                                           |     | (57) |

Averaging against $`p(x)`$ on both sides and cancelling $`c`$ gives the
condition that $`\rho^{*}`$ is the unique root of

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
F(\rho)\;=\;\sum_{x}p(x)\,\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\,\big(\mathbb{E}[r(x,a)]-\rho\,\mathbb{E}[\delta(x,a)]\big)\;=\;0.
``` |  | (58) |

$`F`$ is a maximum of affine functions of $`\rho`$, hence convex,
piecewise linear and strictly decreasing, so the root is unique and we
find $`\rho^{*}`$ by bisection. Empirically, the residual is small
$`|F(\rho^{*})|\sim 10^{-17}`$.

##### Evaluation.

Every instance is run to horizon $`T=30{,}000`$ over all four families,
in two studies whose arm and context counts differ:

- •
  The small-scale study at $`|{\mathcal{X}}|=4`$ with
  $`K\in\{5,10,20,30\}`$.
- •
  The larger-scale study at $`|{\mathcal{X}}|\in\{8,16,32,64\}`$ with
  $`K\in\{70,100,130,160\}`$.

Hyperparameters are selected by grid search on tuning seeds disjoint
from the evaluation seeds, taking the *median* final regret over the
tuning seeds, and the selected configuration is then run on $`100`$
held-out evaluation seeds. Every step that took place counts as part of
the regret calculation, including the burn-in phase (for instance, to
have a nonzero value of counts for C-UCB). Confidence bands are
pointwise percentile bootstraps of the mean over trials.

### C.2 Reward-rate Predictor

We introduce the reward-rate estimator we use for MLE. For $`f_{\rho}`$,
we use a NIW prior with joint Gaussian likelihood ([Murphy,
2012](#bib.bib38)) fitted from historical samples observed in buffer
$`{\mathcal{B}}`$. We model the pair as
$`(r_{\mathrm{acc}},\log\delta_{\mathrm{acc}})`$, where
$`r_{\mathrm{acc}}`$ and $`\delta_{\mathrm{acc}}`$ are the accumulated
reward and time, and we take the logarithm because we need time to be
positive. Writing
$`z_{i}=(r_{\mathrm{acc},i},\,\log\delta_{\mathrm{acc},i})`$ for the
$`i^{\text{th}}`$ of the $`n`$ samples available at step $`t`$, where
$`n`$ is the batch size. The likelihood and its conjugate prior are

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
z_{i}\mid\mu,\Sigma\sim{\mathcal{N}}(\mu,\Sigma),\qquad(\mu,\Sigma)\sim\mathrm{NIW}\big(\mu_{t-1},\,\lambda\kappa_{t-1},\,\lambda\nu_{t-1},\,\lambda\Psi_{t-1}\big),
``` |  | (59) |

where $`\mu_{t-1}`$ is the prior mean of $`\mu`$, $`\Psi_{t-1}`$ is the
prior scatter matrix of $`\Sigma`$, and $`\kappa_{t-1}`$ and
$`\nu_{t-1}`$ are pseudo-counts. The prior at step $`t`$ is the previous
step’s posterior discounted by a forgetting factor $`\lambda\in(0,1]`$,
which shrinks those pseudo-counts so that old evidence decays
geometrically, and the posterior predictive is a Student-$`t`$ with
$`\nu_{t}-1`$ degrees of freedom, where $`\nu_{t}=\lambda\nu_{t-1}+n`$
is the posterior count after this step’s $`n`$ samples are absorbed.
Reward rate is estimated by sampling $`M`$ batches of $`n`$ draws each
from this predictive. Writing the $`m^{\text{th}}`$ batch as
$`\{(x_{m,j},\,y_{m,j})\}_{j=1}^{n}`$, each batch yields one rate, and
$`\hat{\rho}_{t+1}`$ is the 95th percentile of them,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho_{m}=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{m,j}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\exp(y_{m,j})},\qquad\hat{\rho}_{t+1}=\mathrm{Quantile}_{0.95}\big(\{\rho_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M}\big).
``` |  | (60) |

### C.3 MLE-Bench

#### C.3.1 Environment, Reward and Self-improvement

##### Execution.

Every action $`a`$ is a code block generated by the policy (Qwen3.5-4B).
The code block is executed in its own sandbox subprocess environment
with its own working directory, under a memory budget of 16GB and a
compute budget of 2 CPUs. The subprocess is killed when it reaches
timeout $`\delta_{\max}`$. We set $`\delta_{\max}=600`$ seconds, except
for nomad2018, pizza, tabular-2021 and tabular-2022, where the dataset
is large enough that $`600`$ seconds admits almost no honest attempt, so
we use $`\delta_{\max}=1200`$ seconds for these tasks. Time $`\delta`$
is floored at clip_time $`=0.1`$ seconds before it is used anywhere, so
that no sample can claim an unboundedly large rate. We train with a
batch size of 128. Thus, assuming full parallelization at each step, we
require 16$`\times`$128 = 2048GB of memory with 256 CPUs. This amount of
resource is large in academic setting, so we use a first-in-first-out
queue that processes the 128 samples by 16 samples running parallel at a
time through Ray.

##### Reward.

A run is a *valid submission* when the script terminates before
$`\delta_{\max}`$, generates a submission file, and that file is
accepted by the MLE-Bench grader. The grader returns the competition’s
own metric. For the $`15`$ tasks whose metric is higher-is-better and
bounded, we use performance metric (such as AUC) directly as the reward.
For the remaining $`7`$ tasks, where the metric is lower-is-better and
has no bounded value (such as log loss), we use the position of the
submission on the MLE-Bench leaderboard normalized as percentiles as
reward. When there is a tie on the leaderboard, we use the mid-point
position.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r_{t+1}\;=\;\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Big(\mathbbm{1}\{\ell_{i}\prec g\}\;+\;\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbbm{1}\{\ell_{i}=g\}\Big)\;\in\;[0,1],
``` |  | (61) |

where $`\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{N}`$ are the leaderboard entries and
$`\prec`$ orders them in the competition’s own direction. This restores
the higher-is-better direction and bounds the reward in $`[0,1]`$. The 7
tasks using leaderboard score are exactly the seven marked with
$`(\downarrow)`$ in
[Table 1](#S4.T1 "In Reward-rate predictor. ‣ 4.1 Instantiating Language Models for Reward-rate Policies ‣ 4 Reward-rate for MLE Agent ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").

##### Failures.

If a script fails to obtain a valid submission, we define it as a
failure. We use a penalty of $`-10`$ for invalid submissions. Writing
$`s`$ for a valid submission’s score of
[Equation 61](#A3.E61 "In Reward. ‣ C.3.1 Environment, Reward and Self-improvement ‣ C.3 MLE-Bench ‣ Appendix C Implementation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents"),
the reward functions for vanilla and RPG are

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\tilde{r}^{\,\mathrm{RPG}}_{t+1}=\begin{cases}s-\hat{\rho}_{t+1}\,\delta_{t+1},&\text{valid},\\[2.0pt]
-10-\hat{\rho}_{t+1}\,\delta_{\max},&\text{invalid},\end{cases}\qquad\tilde{r}^{\,\mathrm{vanilla}}_{t+1}=\begin{cases}s,&\text{valid},\\[2.0pt]
-10,&\text{invalid}.\end{cases}
``` |  | (62) |

For RPG, we charge $`\hat{\rho}_{t+1}\,\delta_{\max}`$ for invalid
submissions so that every invalid sample’s reward is strict below the
valid one.

##### Self-improvement buffer.

The transition stored in $`{\mathcal{B}}`$ is the extracted code, the
grader’s message, the score $`s`$ of the submission, and the measured
time $`\delta_{t+1}`$. The buffer holds a capacity of 10 times the batch
size, i.e. $`1{,}280`$ solutions. At every step, it is ranked by the
relative reward

|     |                                                              |     |      |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathrm{key}(a,r,\delta)\;=\;r\;-\;\hat{\rho}_{t+1}\,\delta,
       ```                                                           |     | (63) |

with $`\hat{\rho}_{t+1}`$ obtained from the current step’s reward rate
estimate. The vanilla arm uses the identical buffer with
$`\hat{\rho}=0`$. The top $`128`$ solutions ranked by the key fill the
$`128`$ self-improvement prompts of the next step, cycling from the top
when the buffer holds $`<128`$ samples. A valid sample whose score
strictly exceeds every retained solution’s receives an additional
self-improvement bonus of $`0.5`$, which shapes the advantage of both
arms but enters neither
[Equation 63](#A3.E63 "In Self-improvement buffer. ‣ C.3.1 Environment, Reward and Self-improvement ‣ C.3 MLE-Bench ‣ Appendix C Implementation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
nor the rate estimate.

#### C.3.2 Prompts

##### Base prompt.

The initial state $`s_{0}`$ is a chat-formatted prompt carrying the data
path, the task description, the metric, the available packages, the
required submission format, and a schema snippet of the training file.
It also carries the single efficiency instruction referred to in
[Section 4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Instantiating Language Models for Reward-rate Policies ‣ 4 Reward-rate for MLE Agent ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").
See
[Figure 5](#A3.F5 "In Base prompt. ‣ C.3.2 Prompts ‣ C.3 MLE-Bench ‣ Appendix C Implementation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents")
for an example.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 5: Example prompt on MLE-Bench.

##### Self-improvement prompt.

The next state $`s_{t+1}`$ replaces the opening instruction with the
self-improvement phrase $`i_{0}`$ and appends the selected solution and
its grader message. Every other line is byte-identical to the base
prompt, so the two states differ only in what the self-improvement loop
contributes. The differing lines are shown in
[Figure 6](#A3.F6 "In Self-improvement prompt. ‣ C.3.2 Prompts ‣ C.3 MLE-Bench ‣ Appendix C Implementation ‣ Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents").
previous_plan_code is filled with the executed code of the selected
transition, which is the action $`a`$. previous_plan_error contains the
grader’s own message. For a valid submission, previous_plan_error
reports the achieved time $`\delta`$ and performance score $`s`$, which
is how the agent is told the number it is being asked to beat. For an
invalid one, it reports the failure and the traceback. We set the prompt
length to $`2560`$ tokens and response length to $`2500`$ tokens.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 6: Example prompt for self-improvement. previous_plan_code is
filled with the executed code of the selected transition, which is the
action $`a`$. previous_plan_error contains the grader’s own message.
````
